# Most reproduced "organoid-specific" cancer dependencies are consistent with culture-medium effects: a genome-wide attribution of the 2026 organoid dependency catalogues

*Technical note / resource. Draft v2r2, 2026-10-30 (revised after independent skeptical review). Analysis code and tables: `src/medium_attribution_v2.py`, `generations/medium_attribution_v2_*.csv` (see release README).*

## Abstract

Two 2026 Nature studies (Neiswender et al., Broad/NextGen; Herranz-Ors et al., Sanger) published genome-wide CRISPR dependency catalogues for patient-derived organoids and nominated organoid-specific dependencies as candidate drug targets. Because organoid media are defined, serum-free formulations — lipid- and nutrient-poor relative to serum or plasma — some of these dependencies may reflect culture medium rather than tumor biology. Neiswender et al. showed this for sterol-synthesis genes in a 1,000-gene minipool; the genome-wide, per-gene decomposition has not been reported. Here we decompose every organoid-vs-2D differential dependency in the DepMap 26Q3 release using organoid-medium models grown adherent (similar formulation family, no dome), dome-vs-adherent contrasts within organoid medium, and an unrelated serum-free lineage (CNS in Tumor Stem Media), with library (Avana vs Humagne-CD), lineage, and dynamic-range adjustment, on development patients with disjoint held-out-patient confirmation. Of 456 differential dependencies, 84–86% are classified medium-consistent under stated rules (75–82% under heteroscedasticity-robust SEs; bootstrap slope for adherent reproduction 0.90, 95% CI 0.82–0.99); one gene (LSM7) meets symmetric nominal criteria for format association and none do at 5% FDR. Among the Broad catalogue's published gains, 47% are medium-consistent overall and 87% of those that replicate under lineage adjustment; of Herranz-Ors et al.'s 18 headline genes, 8 of 16 present replicate — 5 medium-consistent (the SREBP/sterol axis MVD, IDI1, MBTPS1, MBTPS2, PNKP) and 3 unresolved. Dependency losses behave similarly (84% medium-consistent); the curated ribosomal set shows a relative weakening that survives global corrections in both assays, for which depletion kinetics under fewer doublings is a testable but unproven explanation. These are consistency classifications, not causal proof: adherent comparators cover 6 of 9 lineages (38/68 dome models) and mixed formulations. We release the per-gene table, with bootstrap flag frequencies, so any nominated organoid target can be checked before wet-lab investment.

## Introduction

Organoid dependency maps are being used to nominate targets that 2D screens miss. The interpretive risk is that "organoid-specific" conflates three differences from classical DepMap screens: 3D format (Matrigel domes), defined serum-free medium, and the Humagne-CD CRISPR library. Patients' tumors are perfused with plasma containing LDL cholesterol, fatty acids, heme/iron carriers, and Wnt ligands; organoid media supply few of these. A dependency that exists only because the medium lacks LDL may not hold in vivo; add-back experiments can test LDL limitation in cultured models, while transfer to tumors would remain untested.

What is already established, and not claimed here: Neiswender et al. (Nature 2026) ran a paired minipool 2×2 (format × serum), showed SQLE/MSMO1 dependency is medium-driven, identified seven format-associated genes including the integrins ITGB1/ITGAV/ITGA3, and concluded format has at most modest effects under serum-free conditions; the LDLR/SREBP sterol-starvation response is textbook physiology; Wnt-secretion dependency in Wnt-free formulations is expected. What has not been done: a genome-wide, per-gene attribution of the *published catalogues* — how many nominated hits are consistent with medium effects, which named targets are affected, whether dependency losses behave the same way, and how the apparent weakening of core essentials in dome screens should be interpreted. That quantification is the contribution here; our one format-consistent genome-wide hit and the format-leaning unresolved set (which includes ITGB1) are consistent with, not a rediscovery of, the minipool format findings.

## Results

### Design

From DepMap 26Q3 CRISPR screens passing QC we formed, on development patients (a patient-level hold-out sequestered before analysis; calibration, gene filtering, and imputation use development screens only): organoid-medium dome models (n=68) and organoid-medium *adherent* models (n=9) across 9 lineages; FBS-adherent models in the same lineages (n=207); and CNS models in serum-free Tumor Stem Media vs FBS (n=29 vs 60). Per-gene library bias was removed using 22 development FBS models screened with both Avana and Humagne-CD (all Avana screens in this release are FBS, so no cross-medium invariance of the offset is assumed; transfer across FBS models is). For each gene we estimate four lineage-adjusted contrasts: D (dome organoid medium vs FBS 2D), A (adherent organoid medium vs FBS 2D — formulation family without dome; individual formulations differ), F (dome vs adherent within organoid medium), and S (TSM vs FBS in CNS). Hits (D q<0.01, |Δ|≥0.25) are flagged **medium-consistent** (column `medium_attributable` in the released table) when A reproduces ≥50% of D with nominal p<0.05 and a 90% ratio CI excluding 0, and F does not meet the symmetric criteria; **format_candidate** under the corresponding rule for F (same ratio/CI/nominal-p requirements, plus adherent ratio < 0.25 so the effect is not substantially reproduced without the dome); otherwise unresolved. A strict variant requiring genome-wide F q<0.05 is released alongside (`flag_fdr`). Flags are consistency classifications under these rules, not causal identification: the adherent comparators span 6 of 9 lineages and several formulations, and derivation/selection differences between model populations cannot be excluded by lineage adjustment. Analyses on raw Chronos and dynamic-range-normalized scores agree; normalized is primary.

### Most differential dependencies are medium-consistent, in both directions

We find 249 dependency gains and 207 losses. 86% of gains and 84% of losses are medium-consistent; one gene (LSM7) is a format candidate under symmetric nominal criteria and none at 5% FDR (minimum F q ≈ 1.0, so the FDR statement is about detection power, not absence of format biology — 34 hits have same-direction F/D ≥ 0.5). Slopes of A on D are 0.84 (gains) and 0.86 (losses), versus 0.18/0.17 for F. Under HC3 robust SEs the medium-consistent fractions are 82%/75%. Leave-one-out over the 9 adherent models: slope 0.88–0.92, ≥93.5% of flags retained (F refitted per omission). A joint bootstrap (one model resample shared by calibration and analysis, B=150; identity replicate reproduces point flags exactly) gives A-on-D slope 0.90 [95% CI 0.82–0.99]; per-gene flags are less stable than the slope (72% of hits flagged medium-consistent in ≥50% of replicates; released as bootstrap frequencies), so individual flags should be read with their CIs and frequencies, not as binary truth. Restricting to the six lineages with adherent comparators (38 dome models) leaves the pattern intact (slope 0.89, median ratio 0.89, 90% of subset hits with ratio ≥ 0.5). Disjoint held-out patients (25 domes vs 78 reserved-patient FBS controls, no shared baseline) confirm: dev→held-out slope 0.96 (r=0.97), 100% sign concordance among medium-consistent hits, held-out adherent reproduction slope 0.90 (Fig. 1).

Named medium-consistent gains include the sterol pathway (SQLE Δ=−0.83, adherent ratio 1.08; MSMO1 −0.81, 0.68), fatty-acid synthesis (FASN −0.42, 1.00; ACLY −0.42, 0.91), heme synthesis (ALAS1 −0.42; FECH −0.37), and Wnt secretion/reception (FZD5, LGR4, WLS; ratios 0.91–1.07, absent in TSM — consistent with Wnt-free formulations, though this conflicts with the NextGen minipool at these genes and rests on 9 adherent models).

Expression data (condition-mapped Omics TPM, same contrasts) corroborate the sterol axis on an orthogonal data type: mevalonate-pathway expression rises by median Δ +0.36 against a dependency Δ of −0.38 (SQLE expression +0.75 vs dependency −0.83; LDLR expression +0.61; pathway score −0.01 FBS-adherent, +0.18 organoid-medium adherent, +0.44 domes) — the expected sterol-starvation signature. Heme and fatty-acid synthesis expression move oppositely (−0.47, −0.36), so expression supports the sterol mechanism specifically (genome-wide corr(Δdependency, Δexpression) ≈ 0).

A specificity control comes from plasma-like medium. In Rossiter et al.'s genome-wide K562 screens (RPMI vs human plasma-like medium, both with dialyzed serum — so not an LDL-removal experiment), the HPLM−RPMI shift is genome-wide near-orthogonal to our organoid contrast (r = 0.04), and SQLE is *relatively less* essential in HPLM (Δ +0.44, differential Z +3.8) versus the strongest gain in serum-free organoid medium. Genes relatively more essential in RPMI (Z>3) are enriched for our medium-consistent gains (odds ratio 4.4, prevalence ratio 4.2, Fisher p = 0.007) — medium-associated dependencies appear bidirectional and partly shared: several dependencies strongest in serum-free organoid medium are weaker in physiological than in conventional formulation in this independent system — cross-system concordance, not a shared-mechanism demonstration. (Single genome-wide line; dialyzed serum in both arms.)

### Audit of the published catalogues

Against the Broad study's published organoids-vs-2D table (Mann-Whitney, unadjusted): of 285 published gains (FDR<0.05, Δ<−0.25), 156 (55%) replicate as lineage-adjusted hits on development patients. Medium-consistent are 135 — 47% of the published list, 87% of the replicating subset — with 20 unresolved, 1 format candidate (LSM7), and 129 not reproduced under lineage adjustment (attribution unestablished, not evidence of biology). The 17 strictest gains (FDR<0.01, Δ<−0.5) are 16 medium-consistent, 1 unresolved. Published losses (n=252): 52% medium-consistent overall, 86% of the 153 replicating.

Against Herranz-Ors et al.: their calls are prevalent within their own assay (in their BAGEL binary matrix, collapsing dual-library profiles within model, exclusive genes are depletion-called in a median 80% of organoids and headline genes in 70%; this measures call prevalence, not robustness to threshold choice, which binary calls cannot assess) — the open question is attribution. Of 97 organoid-exclusive genes (93 in the Broad table), 19 replicate as Broad differential hits (14 gains, 5 losses): 14 medium-consistent, 5 unresolved. Of the headline 18 (16 in-table), 8 replicate, all gains: 5 medium-consistent (MVD, IDI1, MBTPS1, MBTPS2, PNKP — the first four are the SREBP/sterol axis; 5/16 in-table, 5/8 of replicating) and 3 unresolved (SCAP, ratio 0.87, fails nominal adherent significance p=0.057; DDX3X and ITGB1, ratios ≤0.35). ITGB1's unresolved, format-leaning status here is consistent with Neiswender et al.'s minipool format finding for integrins.

### Relative ribosomal weakening in organoid screens: depletion kinetics is a testable explanation, not an established one

The strongest individual losses are spliceosome/ribosome subunits (top Δ up to +1.2 raw Chronos). With curated BAGEL reference sets (spliceosome n=35, ribosomal n=38), Broad median Δ is +0.016 (spliceosome) and +0.172 (ribosomal) against +0.031 for the essential-set baseline: weakening is concentrated in subsets of subunits (13/38 ribosomal and 5/35 spliceosome genes are medium-consistent losses), with ribosomal the only complex showing a clear whole-set shift (a small hand-picked panel median reported in our earlier internal analysis, +0.90, overstates the complex-wide effect and is not used). In Broad data the shift is not a whole-screen scale change *as visible after Chronos' per-screen rescaling* (median common-essential Chronos ratio dome/FBS = 1.00; dome screens run longer, 24 vs 21 days), and it reproduces in adherent organoid medium (ribosomal median A +0.20, within-family format contrast −0.01) — but Chronos rescaling also means Broad data cannot speak to global dynamics directly. In Sanger's assay (organoid table 6 LFC vs 930 2D lines), reference-essential depth is 0.63× in organoids; because the two matrices are processed differently (nonessential medians also differ, −0.002 vs +0.121), we treat LFC magnitudes as secondary. On processing-robust within-model percentiles, ribosomal genes are relatively weaker in Sanger organoids (0.021 vs 0.011) while spliceosome genes are not (0.018 vs 0.027); depth-scaled LFC agrees for ribosomal (1.25 vs 1.57 ×depth). Fewer accumulated doublings with slow depletion of long-lived complexes would produce exactly this pattern, but cumulative doublings are recorded for only 1 of 1,241 Broad screens, so the mechanism is untested here and alternatives (e.g. medium-driven turnover changes) remain open. Neither 2026 catalogue reports or adjusts for the weakening; absolute-threshold "organoid-specific essential" calls are exposed to it in both directions (cf. the 5 Herranz-Ors exclusives that are losses in Broad data). As a cross-system control, the mevalonate gain is visible within Sanger's assay (percentile 0.099 in organoids vs 0.394 in Sanger 2D lines).

## Discussion

For target nomination the practical rule is: an organoid-specific dependency in a nutrient-synthesis pathway (sterol, fatty-acid, heme) should be treated as medium-consistent until tested under repletion, because plasma supplies the end products in vivo. The sterol-axis genes on Herranz-Ors et al.'s headline list (MVD, IDI1, MBTPS1/2, SCAP) are exactly this case. Conversely, genes that do not reproduce in adherent organoid medium (DDX3X, ITGB1 among headline genes; COASY, LSM7, UTP4 among Broad published gains) are the better follow-up candidates — with ITGB1 independently format-associated in the NextGen minipool. Dependency losses deserve symmetric caution: weaker ribosomal/spliceosomal dependency in organoid screens should not be read as reduced target relevance until doublings-resolved data exist.

Limitations. (1) Identification: medium consistency is established by reproduction across *different model populations* sharing a formulation family; adherent comparators cover 6/9 lineages and 38/68 domes have same-lineage comparators, formulations are not identical across arms, and derivation/selection differences are not excluded. Causal medium attribution requires perturbation (add-back) experiments. (2) Uncertainty: per-gene flags are materially less stable than the aggregate slopes (bootstrap frequencies released; HC3 fractions 75–82%); the library offset rests on 22 development dual-library models, and the screen-filtered Humagne-only sensitivity has 7 FBS controls (r=0.78 with the main estimate, slope 0.83 — consistent but inconclusive alone). (3) Format power: with 9 adherent models the F contrast detects nothing at 5% FDR; one gene passes symmetric nominal criteria. (4) Sanger analyses use published LFC tables with different processing across matrices; percentile-based results are primary. (5) CPD/doubling data are essentially absent from 26Q3, so deliverable dynamics corrections are limited to dynamic-range normalization and screen days.

Decisive tests. (1) LDL/cholesterol add-back in organoid-medium models should return the mevalonate dependency score toward the FBS baseline and restore LDLR dependency. (2) Statin/SQLE-inhibitor potency should shift ≥5-fold between matched FBS and defined medium, while ITGB1-class candidates should not respond to LDL. (3) Doubling-recorded screens should test whether ribosomal Chronos recovers per doubling. A concrete protocol for (1–2) with pre-agreed falsification criteria accompanies this note.

## Methods (summary)

Screens: DepMap 26Q3 ScreenGeneEffect (Chronos), ScreenSequenceMap QC filters (PassesQC, not drug-treated/engineered, in combined set), ModelCondition formulation/format annotation. Formulation classes: FBS-containing; Tumor Stem Media; organoid-defined (OPAC/organoid formulations). Patient hold-out sequestered prior to analysis (`sequester_patients_v1`); library offset, gene-completeness filtering, imputation, and reference sets use development screens only; held-out evaluation uses disjoint reserved-patient controls (25 domes, 5 adherent vs 78 FBS-adherent), one evaluation run. Library offset: per-gene mean Humagne-CD − Avana across 22 development dual-screened FBS models, applied to Avana (all-FBS) screens. Contrasts: per-gene OLS on model-mean Chronos with lineage dummies; t-based p, Benjamini–Hochberg q per contrast; HC3 robust SEs released and used for a flag sensitivity. Normalization: per screen, nonessential median → 0, common-essential median → −1 (development FBS-adherent-defined sets: 978 essentials, 5,027 nonessentials). Ratio CIs by delta method (shared-baseline covariance omitted, which widens CIs for same-sign candidates conditional on calibration; joint uncertainty is estimated by a bootstrap sharing one model resample between calibration and analysis (B=150, per-hit flag frequencies released; reference sets frozen at point estimates)). Common-support sensitivity restricts to the six lineages with adherent organoid-medium models. Humagne-only sensitivity filters screens before aggregation. Published tables: Broad figshare `organoids_vs_2d_gene_dependency_tests_full.csv`; Herranz-Ors supplementary table 4 (`organoid_core_fitness_genes`) and table 5 binary calls (collapsed within model across libraries); Sanger organoid LFC (supplementary table 6) vs cell-line EssMatrix; Rossiter et al. Table S1 gene scores (PMC8172426). Expression: Omics TPM logp1 mapped to model conditions via embedded ModelConditionID. Code: `src/medium_attribution_v2.py` and companions (`_heldout`, `_loo`, `_boot`, `sanger_direct_check3.py`, `sanger_tables_audit.py`, `panels_curated.py`, `expression_triangulation.py`, `hplm_reverse_test.py`); outputs under `generations/medium_attribution_v2_*` and `release_v1/tables/`.

## References

1. Neiswender et al. A dependency map enhanced with next-generation 3D cancer models. Nature 2026. doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10843-7.
2. Herranz-Ors et al. A tumour-derived organoid biobank maps cancer gene dependencies. Nature 2026. doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10830-y.
3. DepMap 26Q3 release (Chronos gene effects, screen/model-condition metadata).
4. Rossiter NJ et al. CRISPR screens in physiologic medium reveal conditionally essential genes in human cells. Cell Metab. 2021;33(6):1248-1263.e9. doi:10.1016/j.cmet.2021.02.005 (PMC8172426, Table S1).

## Figures
- Fig. 1 (`figures/fig1_attribution.png`): A vs D and F vs D for all hits, colored by flag.
- Fig. 2 (`figures/fig2_weakening.png`): curated-set medians across Broad contrasts; Sanger essential depth and depth-scaled panel ratios.
- Fig. 3 (`figures/fig3_catalogues.png`): flag composition of published hit lists.
- Supplementary: `generations/survivor_candidates_v1.csv` (unresolved hits, least-medium-consistent first), `generations/medium_attribution_v2_boot_freq.csv`, `generations/medium_attribution_v2_loo.json`.

# Novelty audit v8 — sgen003 completion tranche (supersedes v7 search statements; claim unchanged from v4/v5)

## S3 closest code — CONTENT-level (was member-level)
23 Python files extracted by the executed sgen003 ranges (v1 helper; receipt/hash consistency verified post hoc — v1 lacked full structural enforcement, so acquisition-level fail-closed guarantees for those 48 responses remain independently unverified, see acquisition_deviation_v1 + sgen003 scope_deviation). The retained src/zipfetch.py is the SUBSEQUENT hardened implementation (v3: budgets, exact ranges, EOCD/CD/local-header/CRC validation, tested); it does not retrospectively validate the executed transfer. Content screening of the retained, hash-verified Python texts is unaffected by that limitation ( generations/sgen003/s3_code_contents_screen.json + s3_py_contents.json,
237,568 transferred bytes; 308,583 uncompressed Python bytes). Content screen for minipool|growth format|dome|plastic|serum|culture medium|
Chronos_Dome|environmental sensitivity: **zero substantive hits** ("labil" matches only inside
"availability"). The Zenodo package implements expression-model development, blinded prediction,
Sanger evaluation, synthesis, projection, audits — no measured-environmental-lability analysis.

## S1 supplement
MOESM1 Supplementary Information PDF fetched from the official Nature media route (564,382 bytes,
sha256 c8d28259…; generations/sgen003/s1_supplement_receipt.json); cover verified visually.
Lossy text extraction was inadequate for keyword adjudication (custom font encoding) and is NOT
used as absence evidence. Analytical content cross-checked instead via PMC full text, which carries
all Extended Data Fig. 9 legends and the complete minipool narrative (43 minipool mentions):
S1 reports format/medium OLS effects and class variance only — no join to any external organoid
endpoint. PDF figure-panel visual inspection beyond the cover remains outstanding (explicit).

## Omitted bibliography records (reconciled)
generations/sgen003/omitted_refs.json: XML blocks S1 76 / S2 103 / S3 41 vs Europe PMC subsets
72/96/38 (fuzzy title matching, method labeled). Omitted blocks corrected to 4/7/3 with per-record dispositions in omitted_refs_v2.json (identifier-first reconciliation; v8 original counts were fuzzy-matching artifacts):
DepMap portal, Mutect2/GATK methods, protocols.io organoid protocols, SigProfiler, osteosarcoma
preprint, elastic-net and cross-validation methods, the S3 Zenodo package itself (now inspected),
(corrected list in omitted_refs_v2.json; SigProfiler and the integrin/syntaxin papers are NOT omitted — earlier summary text superseded). None is a
measured-lability→displacement analysis. Han et al. 2020 disposition stands on its complete abstract.

## Residual novelty (unchanged, bounded)
Joining measured paired-format lability to external within-organoid displacement, baseline-adjusted,
panel-wide with predeclared δ — not located in S1/S2/S3 texts, S3 code contents, forward/backward
citations, concept/preprint screens, or S1 supplement legends. Still outstanding: exhaustive
screening beyond relevance top-25, PDF panel visuals, non-Europe-PMC sources. C1 adjudication requested.

# Data files associated with A Dependency Map Enhanced with Next-Generation 3D Cancer Models


## Overview ##
This file set includes metadata files (6 files) and analysis result files (29 files) associated with Neiswender, Maffa, Brenan et al. "A Dependency Map Enhanced with Next-Generation 3D Cancer Models" (Nature, 2026). The custom analysis code used for generating these results is available at a GitHub repository (https://github.com/broadinstitute/DepMap-NextGen-Public).  


In addition, raw profiling data of the models (including data for mutation, copy number, gene expression, and gene dependency) and processed data files required for running the custom code are available at DepMap portal (https://depmap.org/portal/data_page/?tab=allData; file set name "NextGen Model Manuscript 2026").


## Metadata Files ##


### minipool_guide_metadata.csv
This table provides the barcode sequence (“Construct_Barcode”) and target gene (“Gene”) for each of the 2000 sgRNAs included in the minipool library. See Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 9a for the schematic and graphical representations of this library, respectively. This library targets 1,000 genes, including 250 test genes, 650 negative control genes, and 100 positive control (i.e., common essential) genes.


### minipool_library_composition.csv
This table shows the membership of each of the nine core functional classes (“Integrin”, “ECM Adhesion”, “Actin Regulation”, “Adherens Junction”, “Tight Junction”, “Lipid Metabolism”, ”Wnt Signaling”, “PI3K mTOR Signaling”, and “Cell Cycle”) targeted by the minipool library. The majority of the test genes of this library belong to one or more of these core functional classes, while the rest of them (“Other”) do not belong to any of these classes but are still included in the library based on specific interests. See Extended Data Fig. 9a for the graphical representations of this library.


### minipool_screen_metadata.csv
This table provides the metadata, including model ID (“DepMap ID”), growth format, and type of culture medium (“Serum status” and “Culture medium”), as well as the QC results for each of the minipool screens (n = 18). These QC results include log2-fold change correlation between the replicates (“replicate LFC correlation”), total sequencing reads (“Total reads”), and two metrics based on the gene effect distributions of negative and positive controls (“NNMD” and “ROC-AUC”).


### minipool_sequence_metadata.csv
This table provides the metadata, including model ID (“DepMap ID”), growth format, and type of culture medium (“Serum status” and “Culture medium”), as well as the QC results for each of the minipool screen sequencing attempts (n = 34). Note that 16 out of the 18 minipool screens were conducted with technical duplicates. One of the replicates (0178_Adh_Nat_Serum_Dome_RepB) was removed from the further analysis due to the low NNMD score. The read count of the PCR products of genomic DNA prepared from Cas12a-null 293T cells that were infected with the minipool library (HEK_CasNull_MP_control) is also displayed.


### model_metadata.csv
This table provides the metadata, including model ID, lineage (“OncotreeLineage”), primary disease (“OncotreePrimaryDisease”), subtype (“OncotreeSubtype”), growth pattern (Adherent, Mixed, Suspension or Unknown for traditional and Dome or Spheroid for NextGen models), as well as the availability of WGS/RNAseq/CRISPR profiling results for the traditional (n = 1685) and NextGen (n = 314) models used in the study. For the models profiled by the CRISPR screen, the screen type (“CRISPRScreenType”), classified into five types based on the model type and culture condition—namely, 2DS (adherent/suspension culture of the traditional cell line models), 2DO (coat culture of the NextGen organoid models), 3DO (dome culture of the NextGen organoid models), 2DN (coat culture of the NextGen CNS models), and 3DN (spheroid culture of the NextGen CNS models)—is also indicated. Note that "GrowthPattern" indicates the format of culture used for the derivation of the respective model, which can be different from the format of culture used for screening and omics profiling (the latter is indicated by "CRISPRScreenType"; also see "Culture Format" column of Supplementary Table 1).


### screen_metadata.csv
This table provides the metadata, including the model ID, library, screen type, model lineage (“OncotreeLineage”), model primary disease (“OncotreePrimaryDisease”), model subtype(“OncotreeSubtype”), and growth pattern, for all the CRISPR screens of traditional (screen n = 1387; PassesQC = “TRUE”) and NextGen (n = 147) models whose results are analyzed in the study. The availability of gene expression (“HasExprData”) and CN data in the corresponding model is also indicated. The screen type was classified into five types based on the model type and culture condition, namely, 2DS (adherent/suspension culture of the traditional cell line models), 2DO (coat culture of the NextGen organoid models), 3DO (dome culture of the NextGen organoid models), 2DN (coat culture of the NextGen CNS models), and 3DN (spheroid culture of the NextGen CNS models). Note that "GrowthPattern" indicates the format of culture used for the derivation of the respective model, which can be different from the format of culture used for screening and omics profiling (the latter is indicated by "ScreenType"; also see "Culture Format" column of Supplementary Table 1).



## Analytical Result Files ##


### biomarker_expression_tumor_vs_normal.csv
For the three representative biomarker-associated dependencies shown in Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 5 (HNRNPH1 and PROX1 expression addiction and ENO1/ENO2 paralog dependency), the expression of the biomarker (HNRNPH1, PROX1 and ENO2, respectively) was compared between the tumor samples and lineage-matched normal samples of the “TCGA TARGET GTEx” cohort downloaded from the Xena browser (https://xenabrowser.net; n = 3192 [normal], 4143 [tumor]; only samples from nine tissue types, biliary tract, colorectal, breast, CNS/brain, esophagus/stomach, ovary, pancreas, prostate and uterus, were analyzed). The sample number (“normalN” and “tumorN”) and mean expression score (“Mean_normal” and “Mean_tumor”) for the normal and tumor groups, as well as the absolute difference in mean expression (“absDelta”), are indicated. Statistical significance of the difference in expression between the two groups was scored using two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (“MWU_p”). Adjusted P-values were calculated on the Mann-Whitney U test P-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure (“MWU_q”).


### celligner_geneset_scores.csv
Expression scores for each of the 41 gene expression meta-programs identified by Gavish et al. (Nature, 2023 [PMID: 37258682]) as well as Basal and Classical programs defined by Moffitt et al. (Nat Genet, 2015 [PMID: 26343385]) were calculated from the gene expression data of the DepMap models (traditional and NextGen; n = 1914) and TCGA-plus tumor samples (n = 12236). See “Scoring the activity of gene-expression MPs” subsection of Methods for the strategy used for the calculation. The scores shown here underlie all the plots involving the meta-program expression scores, including those shown in Figs. 3a,b, 4a-e,g and Extended Data Figs. 6c,d, 7b-j, 8a,b.  


### celligner_nearest_neighbor_table.csv
For each of the DepMap models (n = 1909) and Novartis PDX models (n = 445; Gao et al. Nat Med, 2015 [PMID: 26479923]) (“input”), the identities (sample ID [“target”] and lineage [“target_lineage”]) of the 100 (25 for PDX models) nearest tumor samples (of the TCGA-plus/Met500 cohort [n = 13104]) on the Celligner UMAP embedding were recorded. This file was used for the Celligner-based model lineage prediction (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Figs. 2b,c).


### celligner_prediction_accuracy.csv
For each of the solid tumor models of DepMap NextGen (n = 304), DepMap traditional (n = 1346), and Novartis PDX (n = 443), their lineages were inferred from the lineages of the 25 (or more; indicated in the “neighbors_considered” column) nearest tumor samples on the Celligner embedding. DepMap models of the Ampulla of Vater and Vulva/Vagina lineages were removed from the further analysis due to the scarcity of tumor samples with corresponding lineages (n = 4 and 0, respectively; “immediate_fail”). The scores shown here underlie the Celligner lineage prediction accuracy plots shown in Extended Data Fig. 2a.


### celligner_undiff_cluster.csv
For each of the DepMap traditional (n = 1367) and NextGen models (n = 382), Novartis PDX models (n = 443), and TCGA-plus/Met500 tumor samples (n = 11029) of solid tumors, their residence in the undifferentiated cluster on the Celligner embedding is indicated (“undiff_cluster”). Note that some models have multiple gene expression profiles and the residence in the undifferentiated cluster was recorded per individual profiles. The undifferentiated cluster was defined on the basis of the relative abundance of the DepMap models and TCGA-plus/Met500 tumor samples as well as the mean  HALLMARK_EPITHELIAL_MESENCHYMAL_TRANSITION ssGSEA enrichment score among the DepMap models in the individual clusters identified on Celligner (cluster n = 79). Four clusters (clusters #28, 59, 62 and 67) were collectively designated as “undifferentiated cluster”. See “Lineage prediction with Celligner” subsection of Methods for the details of this procedure. The scores shown here underlie the plots for the proportion of samples in the undifferentiated cluster shown in  Extended Data Fig. 2c.


### expression_addiction_tests_full.csv
For each of the genes scored for both dependency and expression in the NextGen models (gene n = 17889), the Pearson correlation (r) between the dependency and the expression of the dependency gene itself (“NextGenPearsonR”) and the significance of correlation (by two-tailed Pearson correlation; “NextGenPValue”) were calculated. The corresponding Pearson correlation in the traditional models (“TraditionalPearsonR”) was also scored. In addition, the dependency class of the gene based on the dependency profiles across the DepMap NextGen models is indicated (“NextGenDepClass”; see “Classification of dependency profiles” subsection of Methods). Note that only the genes in the three strong dependency classes (“NextGenDepClass” strongly selective, high variance and pan-essential; gene n = 3786) were plotted in Fig. 2a.


### integrin_fak_colocalization_test.csv
To assess the colocalization between integrin subunits (integrin beta1, integrin alphaV) and FAK in the KP3 cells grown in either plastic (2D) or dome (3D) cultures, the images of integrin staining and FAK staining from the same region were loaded onto Fiji (ImageJ ver 1.54p) and the regions of interest (ROIs) were manually defined by drawing boundaries around single cells. Three metrics for protein colocalization—intensity correlation quotient (“Li’s ICQ”; Li et al. J Neurosci, 2004 [PMID: 15102922]), thresholded Manders' Coefficient 1 (“Mander’s tM1”), and Pearson correlation (“PearsonR”)—between the two stainings within the ROI was calculated using the Coloc2 plugin (ver 3.1.0) for Fiji. Data from four sample types ("Class"), integrin alphaV-staining, plastic (AV2D), integrin alphaV-staining, dome (AV3D), integrin beta1-staining, plastic (B12D), and integrin beta1-staining, dome (B13D), are shown Li’s ICQ values are plotted on Extended Data Fig. 10b.


### major_onc_tsg_3d_vs_2d_gene_full.csv
For the oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes (TSGs) that were frequently (> 1%) mutated in the TCGA cohort (n = 40 [oncogene], 50 [TSG]; CDKN2B was removed since this gene was not evaluated in the NextGen model CRISPR screen), their dependency was compared between the 3D organoids cultured as dome (n = 94) and lineage-matched traditional 2D adherent models (n = 433). Statistical significance of the difference in dependency was scored using two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (“MWU_p”). Adjusted P-values were calculated on the Mann-Whitney U test P-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure (“MWU_q”). For the cancer genes whose mutation (hotspot mutation for the oncogenes and damaging mutation for the TSGs) is annotated, the same analysis was conducted after removing the mutant models to see if the differing dependencies between the 2D models and 3D organoids holds even when we focus our analysis to the models with WT alleles of the respective gene (“mutfree_q” and “mf_confirmation”; also see “major_onc_tsg_3d_vs_2d_gene_full.csv”). The scores shown here underlie the plot shown in Extended Data Fig. 8d.


### major_onc_tsg_3d_vs_2d_mutfree_full.csv
For the oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes (TSGs) that were frequently (> 1%) mutated in the TCGA cohort (n = 40 [oncogene], 50 [TSG]), their dependency was compared between the 3D organoids cultured as dome and lineage-matched traditional 2D adherent models after removing the mutant models of the respective gene (see “major_onc_tsg_alteration_matrix.csv”). The numbers of models used in the comparison (i.e., non-mutant models) are shown in the “2D_N” and “3D_N” columns. Statistical significance of the difference in dependency was scored using two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (“MWU_p”). Adjusted P-values were calculated on the Mann-Whitney U test P-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure (“MWU_q”). 


### major_onc_tsg_3d_vs_2d_pathway_full.csv
For the oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes (TSGs) that were frequently (> 1%) mutated in the TCGA cohort (n = 40 [oncogene], 50 [TSG]), we classified them into one of the 10 oncogenic signaling pathways based on the function of the protein they encode. For the groups of oncogenes and the groups of TSGs that belong to the same pathway (13 groups), mean dependency scores for the genes within the same group were calculated for the individual models. Subsequently, the mean dependency scores (i.e., mean of the means) of the NextGen 3D organoids (n = 94) and lineage-matched traditional 2D models (n = 433) were compared. Statistical significance of the difference in mean dependency scores was assessed using two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (“MWU_p”). Adjusted P-values were calculated on the Mann-Whitney U test P-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure (“MWU_q”). The scores shown here underlie the plot shown in Extended Data Fig. 8f.


### major_onc_tsg_alteration_matrix.csv
For each of the oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes (TSGs) that were frequently (> 1%) mutated in the TCGA cohort (n = 40 [oncogene], 50 [TSG]), mutation (hotspot mutation for oncogenes and damaging mutations for TSGs) of the respective gene per individual models in the NextGen 3D organoids (n = 94) and lineage-matched traditional 2D cell lines (n = 433) were scored. The values indicate the allele frequency of the mutations: 0 = no mutation; 1, 0 < (allele frequency) ≤ 0.95; 2, (allele frequency) > 0.95. This matrix was used to remove mutant models in “major_onc_tsg_3d_vs_2d_mutfree_full.csv”.


### minipool_chronos_gene_effects.csv
Chronos gene dependency scores were determined based on the results of the minipool screens (screen n = 18) for each of the 1,000 genes evaluated in these screens (100 positive control genes, 650 negative control genes, and 250 test genes). These Chronos scores provided the basis for the minipool screen analyses whose results are presented in Figs. 5d-g, Extended Data Figs. 9c-g.


### minipool_growth_format_culture_medium_per_class.csv
After calculating the effects of growth formats and culture media on gene dependencies as coefficients of the linear regression model (see “Minipool screen: analysis” subsection of Methods; the coefficient values are shown in “minipool_regression_coefficients. csv”), two analyses were conducted to evaluate the gene class-specific effects of these two components (i.e., growth format and culture medium) of culture conditions: 1) Mann-Whitney U test to compare the distributions of coefficients between in-class and out-of-class test genes for each of the nine core functional classes of minipool targets (results shown in Extended Data Figs. 9f,g); 2) F-test to compare the variances of the coefficients between in-class and out-of-class test genes for each of the nine core functional classes of minipool targets (results shown in Fig. 5g). This table summarizes the results of these two analyses, where columns starting with “GF” indicate the effects of growth formats and those starting with “CM” represent the effects of culture media. The scores shown here underlie the plot shown in Fig. 5g and Extended Data Figs. 9f,g.


### minipool_growth_format_tests.csv
For each of the test genes assessed by the minipool screen (gene n = 250), the effect of the growth formats (Matrigel dome culture [dome] vs monolayer culture on plastic plates [plastic]) on gene dependency was extracted as a coefficient of the linear regression model (see “Minipool screen: analysis” subsection of Methods; these coefficients are shown in “minipool_regression_coefficients. csv”) and the significance of the effect was scored by the two-sided linear regression t-test (“pvalue”). FDR (adjusted P-value) was calculated using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure. The mean Chronos scores in the screens on dome cultures (n = 11) and plastic cultures (n = 7) are also shown (“true_dome_mean” and “true_plastic_mean”, respectively). The scores shown here underlie the plots shown in Fig. 5d and Extended Data Fig. 9f.


### minipool_regression_coefficients.csv
For each of the genes assessed by the minipool screen (gene n = 1000), the effects of the growth formats (Matrigel dome culture [dome] vs monolayer culture on plastic plates [plastic) and the culture media (serum-free OPAC medium vs serum-containing RPMI/FBS medium) on gene dependency were extracted as coefficients of the linear regression model (see “Minipool screen: analysis” subsection of Methods). This spreadsheet shows the coefficients representing the effect of growth formats (“C(Growth_Format)[T.Plastic]”) and the effect of culture media (“C(Serum_status)[T.Serum-free]”) for each gene. The scores shown here underlie the plots shown in Figs 5d-g and Extended Data Figs. 9f,g.


### minipool_regression_pvalues.csv
In extracting the effects of growth formats and culture media on gene dependencies (gene n = 1000) via the linear regression model, the significance of these effects—against the null hypothesis that these components of culture conditions do not have any effect on gene dependency—were also scored using the two-sided linear regression t-test. This spreadsheet shows the P-values for the effect of growth formats (“C(Growth_Format)[T.Plastic]”) and the effect of culture media (“C(Serum_status)[T.Serum-free]”) per each gene. The scores shown here underlie the plots shown in Figs 5d,e.


### minipool_serum_status_tests.csv
For each of the test genes assessed by the minipool screen (gene n = 250), the effect of the culture media (serum-free OPAC medium vs serum-containing RPMI/FBS medium) on gene dependency was extracted as a coefficient of the linear regression model (see “Minipool screen: analysis” subsection of Methods; these coefficients are shown in “minipool_regression_coefficients. csv”) and the significance of the effect was scored by the two-sided linear regression t-test (“pvalue”). FDR (adjusted P-value) was calculated using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure. The mean Chronos scores in the screens with serum-containing RPMI/FBS (n = 9) and serum-free OPAC (n = 9) are also shown (“true_serum_mean” and “true_serum_free_mean”, respectively). The scores shown here underlie the plots shown in Fig. 5e and Extended Data Fig. 9g.


### next_gen_cancer_gene_annotations.csv
For all the oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes (TSGs; both annotated by the OncoKB; https://www.oncokb.org), the number of the NextGen models (with CRISPR profiles [n = 147]) that have relevant alterations—hotspot mutation and/or amplification for oncogenes and damaging mutation and/or deletion for TSGs—were scored. Oncogenes and TSGs with sufficient number of altered NextGen models (n ≥ 5 and at least one model with a hotspot mutation) were subjected to the analysis of dependencies associated with cancer gene alterations (shown in Fig. 2f). These included 6 oncogenes (CTNNB1, EGFR, ERBB2, KRAS, PIK3CA and TERT) and 13 TSGs (APC, ARID1A, CDKN2A, CIC, FBXW7, NF1, PIK3R1, PTEN, RB1, RNF43, SMAD4, TP53 and HLA-B).


### next_gen_dependency_lineage_tests.csv
In the analysis of dependencies associated with cancer gene alterations (shown in Fig. 2f), we tested if the observed association between the cancer gene alteration and dependency was consistently beyond the effects caused by lineage-bias of the cancer gene alteration. Specifically, we computed the differences in mean dependency between NextGen screens in each lineage and the remaining (i.e., out-of-lineage) NextGen screens, only considering lineages which have at least 5 models screened (breast, CNS/brain, colorectal, esophagus/stomach, pancreas and prostate). If the dependency difference observed across the two classes of models distinguished by the presence of a cancer gene alteration was outside the range of all dependency differences observed across all lineages, then we deemed the dependency-biomarker relationship to be driven by the cancer gene alteration. Otherwise, the dependency pattern was attributed to lineage effects. This spreadsheet shows the mean dependency difference between in-lineage vs out-of-lineage groups for each lineage:gene pair (n = 6 [lineage], 5536 [gene]). Also see “Identification of biomarker-associated dependencies” subsection of Methods.


### next_gen_vs_traditional_metaprogram_expression_tests.csv
For each of the 41 gene expression meta-programs identified by Gavish et al. (Nature, 2023 [PMID: 37258682]), the activity of the program was scored in the NextGen (n = 305) and lineage-matched traditional (n = 548) models. The activities of individual programs were then compared between the NextGen and traditional model groups both per lineage and with all the organoid lineages (i.e., all lineages except for CNS/brain) combined. The number of models (“NextGenN” and “TraditionalN”) and the mean expression scores (“NextGenMean” and “TraditionalMean”) for both model groups, as well as the difference in mean expression scores (“MeanDifference”) are indicated. Statistical significance of the difference was scored by two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (“MannWhitneyPValue”) and FDR (adjusted P-value; “MannWhitneyFDR”) was calculated using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure.


### onc_tsg_alteration_dependency_tests_full.csv
For oncogenes and TSGs that have sufficient number of NextGen models (n ≥ 5) with relevant alteration (hotspot mutation and/or amplification for oncogenes and damaging mutation and/or deletion for TSGs) (n = 13 [oncogene], 38 [TSG]), gene dependencies were compared between altered and unaltered NextGen models (n = 147 [model], 5536 [gene]). Mean dependency difference as well as the statistical significance of the difference, assessed by two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test, were scored (“NextGenMeanDifference” and “NextGenMannWhitneyPValue”, respectively). The same comparison of gene dependency was conducted between the altered and unaltered traditional models (model n = 597) and the difference in mean dependency as well as the statistical significance of the difference were scored (“TraditionalMeanDifference” and “TraditionalMannWhitneyPValue”, respectively). Note that in the plot shown in Fig. 2f, only the oncogenes and TSGs that have at least one NextGen model with a hotspot mutation (n = 6 [oncogene], 13 [TSG]) and dependencies in the three strong dependency classes (“NextGenDepClass” strongly selective, high variance and pan-essential; gene n = 3786) were included.


### oncogene_gof_alteration_matrix.csv
For each of the cancer genes (oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes [TSGs]; annotated by the OncoKB; https://www.oncokb.org) (gene n = 741), the NextGen models (n = 147) and lineage-matched traditional models (n = 597) were classified based on the presence or absence of the gain-of-function (GOF) alteration of the gene (hotspot mutation and/or amplification). The values indicate the presence/absence of GOF alteration: 0 = absent; 1 = present. This made a basis for selecting oncogenes with sufficient representation of GOF models among the NextGen cohort (see “nextgen_cancer_gene_annotations.csv”) as well as the analysis for dependencies associated with oncogene GOF (Figs. 2f,g).


### organoids_vs_2d_gene_dependency_tail_enrichment_tests_full.csv
The top 100 genes in either extreme of the distribution of mean dependency differences (3D organoids [n = 94] vs lineage-matched 2D models [n = 433]; gene n = 16691 excluding common essential genes) were combined to form a set of 200 genes with differential dependencies. Gene sets from the Hallmark and KEGG legacy collections were tested for enrichment among this set of 200 differential dependency genes using a hypergeometric test (or one-sided Fisher’s exact test). The number of differential dependency genes within each gene set (“OverlapSize”), the size of the gene set after removing essential genes (“EffectiveSetSize”), the original size of the gene set (“OriginalSetSize”), as well as the odds ratio and P-value from the hypergeometric test (“OddsRatio” and “FishersPValue”, respectively), are indicated. Only gene sets with EffectiveSetSize between 101 and 249 were included in the further analysis. The scores shown here underlie the plot shown in Fig. 5a. Also see “Differential dependency analysis between 3D organoids and 2D models” subsection of Methods. 


### organoids_vs_2d_gene_dependency_tests_full.csv
Gene dependencies were compared between the NextGen models that were grown as 3D organoids (n = 94) vs lineage-matched 2D adherent models (n = 433) (gene n = 18159). Mean dependency difference (“MeanDifference”), the statistical significance of the difference assessed by two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test (“MannWhitneyPValue”), as well as the adjusted P-values calculated by the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure (“MannWhitneyFDR”) were scored. Common essential genes, which were removed from the analysis of differential dependency genes (see “organoids_vs_2d_gene_dependency_tail_enrichment_tests_full.csv”), were also labeled (“DropEssential”). This spreadsheet was used to compile the list of 200 differential dependency genes between 2D and 3D models (see “organoids_vs_2d_gene_dependency_tail_enrichment_tests_full.csv”).


### organoids_vs_2d_top_geneset_similarity_matrix.csv
For the nine gene sets enriched for differential dependency genes (see Fig. 5a), their similarity was assessed by calculating the pairwise overlap coefficient, whose values are shown in this spreadsheet. Gene sets with pairwise overlap similarity > 0.3 (KEGG_FOCAL_ADHESION and KEGG_REGULATION_OF_ACTIN_CYTOSKELETON, HALLMARK_G2M_CHECKPOINT and  HALLMARK_E2F_TARGETS) were merged to form functional clusters, resulting in two merged gene sets ("Adhesion/Cytoskeleton" and "Cell Cycle") and five ("Lipid Metabolism," "mTORC1," "OxPhos," "UV," and "SLE") gene sets that remained separate (see Extended Data Fig. 8h).


### paralog_dependency_tests_full.csv
For all the paralog pairs listed on the Ensembl genome browser 113 (https://www.ensembl.org/) with both genes scored for expression and dependency in the NextGen models (paralog pair n = 60527), we computed the Pearson correlation between the expression scores of one of the genes and dependency scores of the other across the NextGen models (model n = 146) (“NextGenPearsonR”). Statistical significance of the correlation was assessed by two-tailed Pearson correlation (“NextGenPValue”). The expression-dependency correlation of the same paralog pair was also scored in the data from the lineage-matched traditional model cohort (n = 572) and recorded (“TraditionalPearsonR”). Note that only genes in the three strong dependency classes (“NextGenDepClass” strongly selective, high variance and pan-essential; gene n = 3786) were plotted in Fig. 2d.


### pdac_classical_dependency_tests_full.csv
The correlation between gene dependency and expression of the PDAC-classical/MUC program across the cohort of the NextGen organoid models were scored for all the genes (n = 108 [model], 18159 [gene]) (“OrganoidPearsonR”). Statistical significance of the correlation was assessed by two-tailed Pearson correlation (“OrganoidPValue”). The membership in the MSigDB “GOBP: WNT_SIGNALING_PATHWAY” is also indicated (“WntSignaling”). Note that only genes in the three strong dependency classes based on the organoid screen data (“OrganoidDepClass” strongly selective, high variance and pan-essential; gene n = 3521) were plotted in Fig. 4d.


### tda_dependency_classification.csv
The dependency profiles of individual genes across the NextGen models were classified into either of the five classes (Non-dependency, Weakly selective, Strongly selective, High variance and Pan-dependency) based primarily on the strategy described in a prior publication (Krill-Burger et al. Genome Biol, 2023 [PMID: 37612728]) (also see “Classification of dependency profiles” subsection of Methods) (n = 18159 [gene], 147 [model]) (“NextGenClass”). The same classification strategy was also applied to the screens of the NextGen organoids (i.e., NextGen models out of the CNS/brain lineage) (n = 108 [organoid]) (“OrganoidsClass”). The variance of dependency scores as well as the dependency rank of each gene in their 90th percentile least depleted model (used for identifying “Pan-dependency” class; also see Dempster et al., bioRxiv, 2019; https://doi.org/10.1101/720243 for the details) were also recorded based both on the NextGen models dependency scores and organoid dependency scores (“NextGen90%ileLineRank” and “Organoids90%ileLineRank”, respectively).


### tumor_suppressor_lof_alteration_matrix.csv
For each of the cancer genes (oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes [TSGs]; annotated by the OncoKB; https://www.oncokb.org) (gene n = 741), the NextGen models (n = 147) and lineage-matched traditional models (n = 597) were classified based on the presence or absence of the loss-of-function (LOF) alteration of the gene (damaging mutation and/or deletion). The values indicate the presence/absence of LOF alteration: 0 = absent; 1 = present. This made a basis for selecting TSGs with sufficient representation of LOF models among the NextGen cohort (see “nextgen_cancer_gene_annotations.csv”) as well as the analysis for dependencies associated with TSG LOF (Fig. 2f).gene,coefficient,pvalue,log10P,FDR,true_serum_mean,true_serum_free_mean

BODY SECTIONS Comparison of gene dependency profiles between different growth formats of NextGen CNS models and organoidsFor the NextGen CNS tumour models and organoids, the gene dependency profiles were compared between the two different culture conditions used for each of these model groups. Specifically, for the NextGen CNS models, the dependency scores between spheroid culture (n = 14) and coat culture (n = 25) and for organoids, and the dependency scores between Matrigel dome culture (n = 55) and coat culture (n = 14) were compared for every gene assessed in the CRISPR screen of these models (n = 18,159) using two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests (Extended Data Fig. 4h). For the organoids in Matrigel dome cultures, only the models from lineages that have corresponding coat-cultured models (ampulla of Vater, colorectal, oesophagus–stomach, ovary, prostate and uterus) were included in this comparison. Lentiviral production for the minipool screen and its validationLentiviral production was conducted using 293FT cells (Thermo Fisher, R70007) in accordance with the ‘Lentiviral Production in Flasks’ protocol available at the Broad Institute GPP web portal (https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gpp/public/resources/protocols). In brief, the lentiviral particles were generated by the co-transfecting the lentiviral plasmid with a packaging plasmid (psPAX2; 12260, Addgene) and VSV-G envelope (pMD2.G; Addgene, 12259) into 293FT cells using PEIpro transfection reagent (Polyplus, 101000033). The medium was replaced 12 h after transfection, and the virus-containing medium was collected after 36–48 h. Library preparation for minipool screensFor the minipool screens, to evaluate the effects of growth formats and culture media on gene essentiality, we decided to select test genes from nine different functional classes. Most of these gene classes are related to the regulation of adhesion–cytoskeleton, lipid metabolism or other processes highlighted in the systematic comparison of genome-wide CRISPR screen data between 2D models and 3D organoids (Fig. 5a,b). The following gene classes were included: integrin (genes encoding an integrin α or β subunit); ECM adhesion (adhesome, https://adhesome.org/); actin regulation (MSigDB gene set and KEGG regulation of actin cytoskeleton); adherens junction (MSigDB gene set and KEGG adherens junction); tight junction (MSigDB gene set and KEGG tight junction); lipid metabolism (a union of two MSigDB gene sets, Hallmark cholesterol homeostasis and Reactome metabolism of lipids); WNT signalling (MSigDB gene set and GOBP WNT signalling pathway); PI3K–mTOR signalling (MSigDB gene set and Hallmark PI3K–mTOR signalling); cell cycle (MSigDB gene set and GOBP cell cycle); and other genes of particular interest (manual curation). To select 250 test genes from these 9 core functional gene classes, we used the dependency profiles of the gene between 2D models and 3D organoids to prioritize genes that exhibited selective enrichment of dependency in either of these model types. Many of these test genes belong to multiple different classes, and the patterns of membership of individual genes across the nine classes and the number of test genes that exhibit the specific pattern are presented in Extended Data Fig. 9a. We then added 650 non-dependency genes and 100 pan-dependency genes, genes that are universally essential across 2D models and 3D organoids, to compile a list of 1,000 genes (Supplementary Table 3). We subsequently designed 4 enAsCas12a sgRNA sequences for each of these 1,000 genes using the CRISPick web tool (https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gppx/crispick/public), which were assembled into 2 constructs (2 sgRNA sequences for the same gene per construct; 2 constructs per gene) of the pRDA_052 backbone (Addgene, 136474). The resulting library with 2,000 constructs was used for minipool screening. Minipool screeningBefore screening, models were tested for their growth in an alternative medium (1:1 OPAC organoid medium for 2D models and RPMI with 10% FBS for 3D organoids) and with alternative growth format (3D Matrigel dome growth for 2D models and 2D monolayer growth for 3D organoids) for at least two passages. Only the combination of medium type and growth format that enabled a comparable rate of growth with the original conditions (<2-fold difference in the doubling times) and reasonably rapid growth (doubling time <120 h), as well as the original conditions of growth format–culture medium pair, were used for the screening. Moreover, all the models selected for screening were subjected to titrations of library virus and puromycin to determine the dose of virus to achieve optimal infection rates and the concentration of puromycin to kill uninfected cells within 3 days, respectively.For the screen, selected models were infected with the amount of library virus required for infecting 30% of the cells in accordance with the result of virus titration on day 0. The infected cells were selected with the concentration of puromycin determined in the puromycin titration between day 1 and day 4. On day 4, cells were seeded into up to 4 conditions (2D monolayer culture on plastic plates (plastic culture) with RPMI + 10% FBS (RPMI–FBS); plastic culture with 1:1 OPAC; 3D Matrigel dome culture (dome culture) with RPMI + 10% FBS; and dome culture with 1:1 OPAC), depending on how many conditions survived the above-mentioned selection criteria for the respective model. For plastic culture, 2 million cells were resuspended with 10 ml of the respective medium and seeded on a Falcon 100 mm TC-treated cell culture dish (Corning, 53003). For dome culture, 2 million cells were resuspended with 0.5 m of the medium used for the condition and subsequently mixed with 1.5 ml of Matrigel. Approximately 40 domes, each with 50 µl of Matrigel–cell suspension were placed on a 100 mm TC-treated culture dish, which was followed by the incubation of the plate at 37 °C for 30 min to allow the Matrigel to solidify. Subsequently, 10 ml of the culture medium was added before further incubation. We prepared two technical replicates per each condition.These cultures were maintained until day 14 with refreshment of the medium every 3 days. If the culture showed signs of confluency (coverage of more than 80% of the bottom surface by the cells for monolayer culture on plastic plates and appearance of a dark spot in the middle of the domes for Matrigel dome culture), we passaged the cells instead of replacing the medium while keeping the number of cells after passaging to 2 million cells per dish. Trypsinization (with 0.25% trypsin and 0.1% EDTA (Corning, 25-053-CI)) was used for the passaging of cells in plastic cultures, whereas cells in dome cultures were passaged in accordance with the strategy described above in the section ‘Source and culture conditions of NextGen cancer models’. At day 14, cells were collected by trypsinization and counted. gDNA samples were prepared from these cells and the abundance of individual sgRNA sequences in the genome of these cells were analysed by PCR amplification of the sgRNA sequences, preparation of sequencing libraries from the PCR products and subsequent sequencing of these libraries as described in the section ‘Genome-wide CRISPR screening for gDNA isolation and sequencing’. Minipool screen analysisMinipool screens were evaluated for sequencing quality by having a total read count of at least 500,000 reads across replicates. Gene scores and NNMDs were computed in the same manner as the genome-wide screens. Replicate correlation was computed as the Pearson’s correlation coefficient over log fold changes in all non-control genes. Screens with NNMDs greater than –1.5 and replicate correlations less than 0.2 were excluded from downstream analyses. Screens with a single replicate were retained if their other metrics passed these quality control thresholds. Chronos scores were calculated as previously described23, with adjusted hyperparameters (smoothing regularization parameter = 0.3, kernel width = 5) for the smaller library size. Subsequently, we modelled the Chronos score Yg,k for each gene g and screen k with the generalized linear regression model:\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${Y}_{g,k}={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{d}{I}_{d}+{\beta }_{s}{I}_{s}+{\beta }_{{ds}}{I}_{d}{I}_{s}+\sum _{m\in M}{\beta }_{m}{I}_{m}$$\end{document}Yg,k=β0+βdId+βsIs+βdsIdIs+∑m∈MβmImThe first term captures the baseline viability effect of knocking out gene g. The second and third terms capture the growth format effect and medium effect, where Id and Is are indicator variables representing the types of growth format (Matrigel dome culture (dome) versus monolayer culture on plastic plates (plastic)) and culture medium (serum-free OPAC medium versus serum-containing RPMI–FBS medium), respectively. The fourth term captures interaction effects between these two conditions, and the final term captures model effects to account for multiple screens in the same cell line. Differences in effect sizes across growth format and serum status were extracted as βd and βs, respectively. Significance values corresponding to the same coefficients were extracted from the P values calculated using two-sided linear regression t-test.To assess the effects of growth format (or culture medium) on the core functional classes of gene targets included in our minipool library, we calculated the variance in βd (or βs) across members of the same class and compared it to the variance in βd (or βs) across all non-control genes outside of class. For each gene set, we tested whether the in-class variance was significantly greater than the out-of-class variance using one-tailed F-tests. 1	# Most reproduced "organoid-specific" cancer dependencies are consistent with culture-medium effects: a genome-wide attribution of the 2026 organoid dependency catalogues
     2	
     3	*Technical note / resource. Draft v2r2, 2026-10-30 (revised after independent skeptical review). Analysis code and tables: `src/medium_attribution_v2.py`, `generations/medium_attribution_v2_*.csv` (see release README).*
     4	
     5	## Abstract
     6	
     7	Two 2026 Nature studies (Neiswender et al., Broad/NextGen; Herranz-Ors et al., Sanger) published genome-wide CRISPR dependency catalogues for patient-derived organoids and nominated organoid-specific dependencies as candidate drug targets. Because organoid media are defined, serum-free formulations — lipid- and nutrient-poor relative to serum or plasma — some of these dependencies may reflect culture medium rather than tumor biology. Neiswender et al. showed this for sterol-synthesis genes in a 1,000-gene minipool; the genome-wide, per-gene decomposition has not been reported. Here we decompose every organoid-vs-2D differential dependency in the DepMap 26Q3 release using organoid-medium models grown adherent (similar formulation family, no dome), dome-vs-adherent contrasts within organoid medium, and an unrelated serum-free lineage (CNS in Tumor Stem Media), with library (Avana vs Humagne-CD), lineage, and dynamic-range adjustment, on development patients with disjoint held-out-patient confirmation. Of 456 differential dependencies, 84–86% are classified medium-consistent under stated rules (75–82% under heteroscedasticity-robust SEs; bootstrap slope for adherent reproduction 0.90, 95% CI 0.82–0.99); one gene (LSM7) meets symmetric nominal criteria for format association and none do at 5% FDR. Among the Broad catalogue's published gains, 47% are medium-consistent overall and 87% of those that replicate under lineage adjustment; of Herranz-Ors et al.'s 18 headline genes, 8 of 16 present replicate — 5 medium-consistent (the SREBP/sterol axis MVD, IDI1, MBTPS1, MBTPS2, PNKP) and 3 unresolved. Dependency losses behave similarly (84% medium-consistent); the curated ribosomal set shows a relative weakening that survives global corrections in both assays, for which depletion kinetics under fewer doublings is a testable but unproven explanation. These are consistency classifications, not causal proof: adherent comparators cover 6 of 9 lineages (38/68 dome models) and mixed formulations. We release the per-gene table, with bootstrap flag frequencies, so any nominated organoid target can be checked before wet-lab investment.
     8	
     9	## Introduction
    10	
    11	Organoid dependency maps are being used to nominate targets that 2D screens miss. The interpretive risk is that "organoid-specific" conflates three differences from classical DepMap screens: 3D format (Matrigel domes), defined serum-free medium, and the Humagne-CD CRISPR library. Patients' tumors are perfused with plasma containing LDL cholesterol, fatty acids, heme/iron carriers, and Wnt ligands; organoid media supply few of these. A dependency that exists only because the medium lacks LDL may not hold in vivo; add-back experiments can test LDL limitation in cultured models, while transfer to tumors would remain untested.
    12	
    13	What is already established, and not claimed here: Neiswender et al. (Nature 2026) ran a paired minipool 2×2 (format × serum), showed SQLE/MSMO1 dependency is medium-driven, identified seven format-associated genes including the integrins ITGB1/ITGAV/ITGA3, and concluded format has at most modest effects under serum-free conditions; the LDLR/SREBP sterol-starvation response is textbook physiology; Wnt-secretion dependency in Wnt-free formulations is expected. What has not been done: a genome-wide, per-gene attribution of the *published catalogues* — how many nominated hits are consistent with medium effects, which named targets are affected, whether dependency losses behave the same way, and how the apparent weakening of core essentials in dome screens should be interpreted. That quantification is the contribution here; our one format-consistent genome-wide hit and the format-leaning unresolved set (which includes ITGB1) are consistent with, not a rediscovery of, the minipool format findings.
    14	
    15	## Results
    16	
    17	### Design
    18	
    19	From DepMap 26Q3 CRISPR screens passing QC we formed, on development patients (a patient-level hold-out sequestered before analysis; calibration, gene filtering, and imputation use development screens only): organoid-medium dome models (n=68) and organoid-medium *adherent* models (n=9) across 9 lineages; FBS-adherent models in the same lineages (n=207); and CNS models in serum-free Tumor Stem Media vs FBS (n=29 vs 60). Per-gene library bias was removed using 22 development FBS models screened with both Avana and Humagne-CD (all Avana screens in this release are FBS, so no cross-medium invariance of the offset is assumed; transfer across FBS models is). For each gene we estimate four lineage-adjusted contrasts: D (dome organoid medium vs FBS 2D), A (adherent organoid medium vs FBS 2D — formulation family without dome; individual formulations differ), F (dome vs adherent within organoid medium), and S (TSM vs FBS in CNS). Hits (D q<0.01, |Δ|≥0.25) are flagged **medium-consistent** (column `medium_attributable` in the released table) when A reproduces ≥50% of D with nominal p<0.05 and a 90% ratio CI excluding 0, and F does not meet the symmetric criteria; **format_candidate** under the corresponding rule for F (same ratio/CI/nominal-p requirements, plus adherent ratio < 0.25 so the effect is not substantially reproduced without the dome); otherwise unresolved. A strict variant requiring genome-wide F q<0.05 is released alongside (`flag_fdr`). Flags are consistency classifications under these rules, not causal identification: the adherent comparators span 6 of 9 lineages and several formulations, and derivation/selection differences between model populations cannot be excluded by lineage adjustment. Analyses on raw Chronos and dynamic-range-normalized scores agree; normalized is primary.
    20	
    21	### Most differential dependencies are medium-consistent, in both directions
    22	
    23	We find 249 dependency gains and 207 losses. 86% of gains and 84% of losses are medium-consistent; one gene (LSM7) is a format candidate under symmetric nominal criteria and none at 5% FDR (minimum F q ≈ 1.0, so the FDR statement is about detection power, not absence of format biology — 34 hits have same-direction F/D ≥ 0.5). Slopes of A on D are 0.84 (gains) and 0.86 (losses), versus 0.18/0.17 for F. Under HC3 robust SEs the medium-consistent fractions are 82%/75%. Leave-one-out over the 9 adherent models: slope 0.88–0.92, ≥93.5% of flags retained (F refitted per omission). A joint bootstrap (one model resample shared by calibration and analysis, B=150; identity replicate reproduces point flags exactly) gives A-on-D slope 0.90 [95% CI 0.82–0.99]; per-gene flags are less stable than the slope (72% of hits flagged medium-consistent in ≥50% of replicates; released as bootstrap frequencies), so individual flags should be read with their CIs and frequencies, not as binary truth. Restricting to the six lineages with adherent comparators (38 dome models) leaves the pattern intact (slope 0.89, median ratio 0.89, 90% of subset hits with ratio ≥ 0.5). Disjoint held-out patients (25 domes vs 78 reserved-patient FBS controls, no shared baseline) confirm: dev→held-out slope 0.96 (r=0.97), 100% sign concordance among medium-consistent hits, held-out adherent reproduction slope 0.90 (Fig. 1).
    24	
    25	Named medium-consistent gains include the sterol pathway (SQLE Δ=−0.83, adherent ratio 1.08; MSMO1 −0.81, 0.68), fatty-acid synthesis (FASN −0.42, 1.00; ACLY −0.42, 0.91), heme synthesis (ALAS1 −0.42; FECH −0.37), and Wnt secretion/reception (FZD5, LGR4, WLS; ratios 0.91–1.07, absent in TSM — consistent with Wnt-free formulations, though this conflicts with the NextGen minipool at these genes and rests on 9 adherent models).
    26	
    27	Expression data (condition-mapped Omics TPM, same contrasts) corroborate the sterol axis on an orthogonal data type: mevalonate-pathway expression rises by median Δ +0.36 against a dependency Δ of −0.38 (SQLE expression +0.75 vs dependency −0.83; LDLR expression +0.61; pathway score −0.01 FBS-adherent, +0.18 organoid-medium adherent, +0.44 domes) — the expected sterol-starvation signature. Heme and fatty-acid synthesis expression move oppositely (−0.47, −0.36), so expression supports the sterol mechanism specifically (genome-wide corr(Δdependency, Δexpression) ≈ 0).
    28	
    29	A specificity control comes from plasma-like medium. In Rossiter et al.'s genome-wide K562 screens (RPMI vs human plasma-like medium, both with dialyzed serum — so not an LDL-removal experiment), the HPLM−RPMI shift is genome-wide near-orthogonal to our organoid contrast (r = 0.04), and SQLE is *relatively less* essential in HPLM (Δ +0.44, differential Z +3.8) versus the strongest gain in serum-free organoid medium. Genes relatively more essential in RPMI (Z>3) are enriched for our medium-consistent gains (odds ratio 4.4, prevalence ratio 4.2, Fisher p = 0.007) — medium-associated dependencies appear bidirectional and partly shared: several dependencies strongest in serum-free organoid medium are weaker in physiological than in conventional formulation in this independent system — cross-system concordance, not a shared-mechanism demonstration. (Single genome-wide line; dialyzed serum in both arms.)
    30	
    31	### Audit of the published catalogues
    32	
    33	Against the Broad study's published organoids-vs-2D table (Mann-Whitney, unadjusted): of 285 published gains (FDR<0.05, Δ<−0.25), 156 (55%) replicate as lineage-adjusted hits on development patients. Medium-consistent are 135 — 47% of the published list, 87% of the replicating subset — with 20 unresolved, 1 format candidate (LSM7), and 129 not reproduced under lineage adjustment (attribution unestablished, not evidence of biology). The 17 strictest gains (FDR<0.01, Δ<−0.5) are 16 medium-consistent, 1 unresolved. Published losses (n=252): 52% medium-consistent overall, 86% of the 153 replicating.
    34	
    35	Against Herranz-Ors et al.: their calls are prevalent within their own assay (in their BAGEL binary matrix, collapsing dual-library profiles within model, exclusive genes are depletion-called in a median 80% of organoids and headline genes in 70%; this measures call prevalence, not robustness to threshold choice, which binary calls cannot assess) — the open question is attribution. Of 97 organoid-exclusive genes (93 in the Broad table), 19 replicate as Broad differential hits (14 gains, 5 losses): 14 medium-consistent, 5 unresolved. Of the headline 18 (16 in-table), 8 replicate, all gains: 5 medium-consistent (MVD, IDI1, MBTPS1, MBTPS2, PNKP — the first four are the SREBP/sterol axis; 5/16 in-table, 5/8 of replicating) and 3 unresolved (SCAP, ratio 0.87, fails nominal adherent significance p=0.057; DDX3X and ITGB1, ratios ≤0.35). ITGB1's unresolved, format-leaning status here is consistent with Neiswender et al.'s minipool format finding for integrins.
    36	
    37	### Relative ribosomal weakening in organoid screens: depletion kinetics is a testable explanation, not an established one
    38	
    39	The strongest individual losses are spliceosome/ribosome subunits (top Δ up to +1.2 raw Chronos). With curated BAGEL reference sets (spliceosome n=35, ribosomal n=38), Broad median Δ is +0.016 (spliceosome) and +0.172 (ribosomal) against +0.031 for the essential-set baseline: weakening is concentrated in subsets of subunits (13/38 ribosomal and 5/35 spliceosome genes are medium-consistent losses), with ribosomal the only complex showing a clear whole-set shift (a small hand-picked panel median reported in our earlier internal analysis, +0.90, overstates the complex-wide effect and is not used). In Broad data the shift is not a whole-screen scale change *as visible after Chronos' per-screen rescaling* (median common-essential Chronos ratio dome/FBS = 1.00; dome screens run longer, 24 vs 21 days), and it reproduces in adherent organoid medium (ribosomal median A +0.20, within-family format contrast −0.01) — but Chronos rescaling also means Broad data cannot speak to global dynamics directly. In Sanger's assay (organoid table 6 LFC vs 930 2D lines), reference-essential depth is 0.63× in organoids; because the two matrices are processed differently (nonessential medians also differ, −0.002 vs +0.121), we treat LFC magnitudes as secondary. On processing-robust within-model percentiles, ribosomal genes are relatively weaker in Sanger organoids (0.021 vs 0.011) while spliceosome genes are not (0.018 vs 0.027); depth-scaled LFC agrees for ribosomal (1.25 vs 1.57 ×depth). Fewer accumulated doublings with slow depletion of long-lived complexes would produce exactly this pattern, but cumulative doublings are recorded for only 1 of 1,241 Broad screens, so the mechanism is untested here and alternatives (e.g. medium-driven turnover changes) remain open. Neither 2026 catalogue reports or adjusts for the weakening; absolute-threshold "organoid-specific essential" calls are exposed to it in both directions (cf. the 5 Herranz-Ors exclusives that are losses in Broad data). As a cross-system control, the mevalonate gain is visible within Sanger's assay (percentile 0.099 in organoids vs 0.394 in Sanger 2D lines).
    40	
    41	## Discussion
    42	
    43	For target nomination the practical rule is: an organoid-specific dependency in a nutrient-synthesis pathway (sterol, fatty-acid, heme) should be treated as medium-consistent until tested under repletion, because plasma supplies the end products in vivo. The sterol-axis genes on Herranz-Ors et al.'s headline list (MVD, IDI1, MBTPS1/2, SCAP) are exactly this case. Conversely, genes that do not reproduce in adherent organoid medium (DDX3X, ITGB1 among headline genes; COASY, LSM7, UTP4 among Broad published gains) are the better follow-up candidates — with ITGB1 independently format-associated in the NextGen minipool. Dependency losses deserve symmetric caution: weaker ribosomal/spliceosomal dependency in organoid screens should not be read as reduced target relevance until doublings-resolved data exist.
    44	
    45	Limitations. (1) Identification: medium consistency is established by reproduction across *different model populations* sharing a formulation family; adherent comparators cover 6/9 lineages and 38/68 domes have same-lineage comparators, formulations are not identical across arms, and derivation/selection differences are not excluded. Causal medium attribution requires perturbation (add-back) experiments. (2) Uncertainty: per-gene flags are materially less stable than the aggregate slopes (bootstrap frequencies released; HC3 fractions 75–82%); the library offset rests on 22 development dual-library models, and the screen-filtered Humagne-only sensitivity has 7 FBS controls (r=0.78 with the main estimate, slope 0.83 — consistent but inconclusive alone). (3) Format power: with 9 adherent models the F contrast detects nothing at 5% FDR; one gene passes symmetric nominal criteria. (4) Sanger analyses use published LFC tables with different processing across matrices; percentile-based results are primary. (5) CPD/doubling data are essentially absent from 26Q3, so deliverable dynamics corrections are limited to dynamic-range normalization and screen days.
    46	
    47	Decisive tests. (1) LDL/cholesterol add-back in organoid-medium models should return the mevalonate dependency score toward the FBS baseline and restore LDLR dependency. (2) Statin/SQLE-inhibitor potency should shift ≥5-fold between matched FBS and defined medium, while ITGB1-class candidates should not respond to LDL. (3) Doubling-recorded screens should test whether ribosomal Chronos recovers per doubling. A concrete protocol for (1–2) with pre-agreed falsification criteria accompanies this note.
    48	
    49	## Methods (summary)
