CNS models were screened as spheroids or on matrix-coated plates (termed ‘coat’ hereafter) and organoids were screened in Matrigel domes or in coat conditions, all in serum-free media (Supplementary Table 1). Gene expression and essentiality profiles were nearly identical across CNS growth formats (Pearson’s r = 0.996 and 0.990, respectively), and organoid gene dependencies also strongly agreed between the two conditions (r = 0.984; Extended Data Fig. 4c–h). These results suggest that growth format does not significantly affect CRISPR screen outcomes under serum-free conditions. This finding is in contrast to a previous study that used serum-containing media22—a discrepancy that may be attributable to differences in medium composition and the comparison strategy used. All models were profiled for WGS, RNA-seq and CRISPR under identical conditions.
To validate these findings, we knocked out ITB1, ITGAV, MSMO1 or SQLE in KP3 and HS766T pancreas models under 2D plastic (with RPMI–FBS) and 3D dome (with RPMI–FBS or OPAC) cultures. Cholesterol biosynthesis gene dependencies (MSMO1 and SQLE) varied by medium, whereas integrin subunit dependencies (ITGAV and ITGB1) were sensitive to growth format (Fig. 5h and Extended Data Fig. 10a). Immunofluorescence analyses confirmed that integrin β1 (encoded by ITGB1) colocalized with FAK in 3D but not 2D cultures, whereas integrin αV (encoded by ITGAV) showed enhanced FAK colocalization in 2D relative to 3D cultures, which was partially due to reduced cell surface expression in 3D (Fig. 5i and Extended Data Fig. 10b–e). These findings align with their differential roles in cell–ECM interactions across different growth formats55.
Our data also revealed that oncogenic signalling roles differ significantly between model types. WNT signalling is required for organoids with a PDAC-classical/MUC program but is largely dispensable in traditional models (Fig. 4). By contrast, dependencies on ESR1 and ERBB2 were exclusive to traditional cell lines (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 5b,d), which probably stem from reduced expression of these oncogenes in the organoids (Extended Data Fig. 5d) owing to composition differences in the media. Together, these findings demonstrate that multiple oncogenic signalling pathways are highly context-dependent, which reinforces the fact that cellular microenvironments substantially shape requirements for these pathways56,57.
Cell lines with Cas activity above 70% were selected for screening. However, some lines were screened with activity as low as 44% if they showed sufficiently rapid growth of at least one population doubling per week.
CNS models were tested for the growth format and seeding density that resulted in optimal growth rates and for polybrene sensitivity, which was used at a concentration that resulted in >85% survival. For growth testing, cells were plated in both Matrigel-coated and ULA 6-well tissue culture plates. Specifically, cells were seeded in duplicate at densities of 100,000, 200,000 and 300,000 cells per well for both the Matrigel-coated plates and ULA plates. Cells were allowed to grow for 7 days, with a medium change performed at day 3 or 4 as needed. After 7 days, cells from all the conditions were counted and a doubling time was calculated for each condition. The condition that gave the lowest doubling time while maintaining high cell viability was used for the screen. Blasticidin and puromycin were used at a standardized concentration of 50 µg ml–1 and 3 µg ml–1, respectively. For enAsCas12a transduction, 1.5 × 106 cells were exposed to lentivirus expressing enAsCas12ain a 24-well ULA plate in the presence of the optimized concentration of polybrene. At 18 h after infection, cells were washed with PBS to remove the virus and the cells were plated in the optimal growth format at 2× the optimal seeding density. Subsequently, cells were selected with blasticidin. A CellTiter-Glo cell viability assay (CTG; Promega, G7572) was carried out 14 days after infection to ensure efficient elimination of uninfected cells with blasticidin and to measure the infection rate from the enAsCas12a virus.
For the CRISPR screens of the traditional cancer cell lines with the enAsCas12a sgRNA library (Humagne-CD), the cell lines were first tested for doubling time and cell size. Blasticidin and puromycin were used at a standard concentration of 40 μg ml–1 and 2 μg ml–1, respectively. To infect adherent cells with lentivirus expressing enAsCas12a (Addgene, 136476), 5 × 106 cells were exposed to the virus in a T175 flask (Corning, 354487) in the presence of 4 µg ml–1 polybrene. For suspension cells, 1.8 × 107 cells were exposed to the virus in a 12-well plate (Corning, 3513) in the presence of 4 µg ml–1 polybrene, which was followed by centrifugation at 930g, 37 °C for 2 h. One day after infection, cells were washed with PBS to remove the virus and cells were then plated at around 50% confluence. Blasticidin was added to the medium 2–3 days after infection. A CTG assay was carried out after 3 days of blasticidin selection to ensure efficient elimination of uninfected cells with blasticidin and to estimate the infection rate from the enAsCas12a virus. Cells were maintained in blasticidin for at least 10 days after transduction and throughout the screening process. After enCas12a transduction and blasticidin selection, enCas12a activity was assessed as described in the section ‘Genome-wide CRISPR screening of organoids’.
Before screening, models were tested for their growth in an alternative medium (1:1 OPAC organoid medium for 2D models and RPMI with 10% FBS for 3D organoids) and with alternative growth format (3D Matrigel dome growth for 2D models and 2D monolayer growth for 3D organoids) for at least two passages. Only the combination of medium type and growth format that enabled a comparable rate of growth with the original conditions (<2-fold difference in the doubling times) and reasonably rapid growth (doubling time <120 h), as well as the original conditions of growth format–culture medium pair, were used for the screening. Moreover, all the models selected for screening were subjected to titrations of library virus and puromycin to determine the dose of virus to achieve optimal infection rates and the concentration of puromycin to kill uninfected cells within 3 days, respectively.
The viability effect (10 days after sgRNA transduction) of CRISPR-mediated knockout of ITGB1, ITGAV, MSMO1 and SQLE (Fig. 5h and Extended Data Fig. 10a) was assessed using CTG cell viability assays. Specifically, KP3 and HS766T pancreatic cancer cells, both of which were engineered to express enAsCas12a, were infected with several different types of sgRNA-expressing lentivirus on day 0, which included CRISPR cutting controls (sgCh2 and sgAAVS1), sgRNAs targeting common essential genes (sgPOLR2D, sgSF3B1 and sgKIF11) and sgRNAs against the experimental genes (sgITGB1, sgITGAV, sgMSMO1 and sgSQLE). The infected cells were selected with 2 μg ml–1 puromycin between day 1 and day 3. On day 3, cells were trypsinized, counted and reseeded without puromycin. For the 2D monolayer culture on a plastic plate (or plastic culture), cells were seeded at 2,000 cells per well in 100 µl RPMI medium with 10% FBS onto an opaque 96-well plate (Corning, 3903). For the 3D Matrigel dome culture (or dome culture), 10,000 cells were resuspended with 50 μl Matrigel and plated as a dome onto a 12-well plate, which was subsequently incubated (Corning, 356231) at 37 °C for 30 min to allow the Matrigel to solidify. The Matrigel dome was then covered with 1,200 μl per well of either the RPMI medium with 10% FBS or the 1:1 OPAC medium before further incubation. The medium was replaced every 3 days until day 10. Puromycin (2 μg ml–1) was added back to the culture at the first medium replacement.
For Fig. 5h, the effects of growth formats on the viability of KP3 and HS766T cells following integrin (ITGB1 and ITGAV) knockout, as well as the effects of culture media on the viability of these cells following the knockout of cholesterol synthesis mediators (MSMO1 and SQLE), were analysed by two-tailed two-way ANOVA. The viability of the KP3 and HS766T cells following gene knockout was measured as triplicates.

Extended Data Fig. 4Comparison of gene expression and CRISPR screen outcomes between 2D and 3D cultures.a,b, CRISPR screen QC metrics. In a, ROC-AUC (Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve) scores for common essential (positive controls; defined as the intersection of essential genes in Hart et al.70 and Blomen et al.71) and nonessential (negative controls; defined by Hart et al.70) controls were calculated using the naïve gene effect scores and plotted for all the DepMap CRISPR screens. In b, NNMD (Null-Normalized Median Difference) score between the common essential and nonessential controls was calculated for each screen. The screens evaluated here included Cas9 traditional model screens (n = 1,351), enAsCas12a traditional model screens (n = 36), enAsCas12a NextGen organoid screens (n = 108), and enCas12a NextGen CNS model screens (n = 39). For both metrics, scores from the NextGen models were comparable to those from the Cas9 traditional model screens and enAsCas12a traditional model screens. The centre (for consistency with the main text) line and box denote median and 25th to 75th percentile data points, respectively, and whiskers extend up to 1.5 times the interquartile range from box edges. c,d, Clustering of samples from NextGen CNS tumor models in 3D spheroid culture and 2D adherent culture on Matrigel-coated plates (“coat” culture) by the correlation of gene expression. Nine NextGen CNS tumor spheroid models were either maintained in the spheroid culture or propagated in the coat culture for > 4 weeks. In c, gene expression profiles of these 18 samples (9 models x 2 conditions) were compared and clustered using the correlation of expression across top 10% highly variable genes (n = 1,919). These samples were primarily clustered by cell identity, but not by the culture conditions. The distributions of correlation between two different samples were also plotted (d), exhibiting the high degree of correlation (r > 0.8) between two samples with different conditions (spheroid and adherent cultures) of the same model. P-values were calculated with two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test. n = 9 (same model under coat and spheroid culture conditions), 72 (different models under different culture conditions), 36 (different models both in coat cultures), and 36 (different models both in spheroid cultures). e,f, High concordance of gene expression between spheroid and coat cultures of the NextGen CNS models. The mean expression levels in the nine spheroid culture samples (x-axis) and the nine coat culture samples (y-axis) were plotted for all the genes (n = 19,193), which exhibited a very high degree of concordance (r = 0.996) between these two culture conditions (e). The difference in the mean expression levels (x-axis) and the statistical significance of the difference (by a two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test; y-axis) were also plotted (f). The false discovery rate (FDR; q) was 1 for all the genes, indicating that none of the genes exhibited statistically significant differences. g,h Concordance of Chronos dependency scores between 3D culture and 2D coat culture. The mean dependency scores of each gene in the NextGen CNS models screened under 3D spheroid cultures (n = 14; x-axis) and in the NextGen CNS models screened under adherent cultures on laminin- or Matrigel-coated plates (“coat” cultures; n = 25; y-axis) were plotted (g, left). Similarly, the mean dependency scores of genes in the organoid models screened under 3D Matrigel dome cultures (n = 55; x-axis) and in the organoid models screened under coat cultures (n = 14; y-axis) were plotted (g, right). For the organoids in Matrigel dome cultures, only the models from lineages that have corresponding coat-cultured models (ampulla of vator, colorectal, oeso-stm, ovary, prostate and uterus) were included in this comparison. In both cases, a high degree of concordance was observed between the two different conditions of culture (r = 0.990 and 0.984 for CNS models and organoids, respectively). The difference in the mean dependency scores between the spheroid and coat culture of the CNS models (h, left) and between the dome and coat cultures of the organoid models (h, right) (x-axis) and the significance of the difference (y-axis; by a two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test) were also plotted. In both cases, none of the genes exhibited a statistically significant difference of the mean dependency scores between two different culture conditions (q = 1 for all the genes [CNS]; q > 0.71 for all the genes [organoids]). Note that gene expression comparison between spheroid and coat cultures of the NextGen CNS models (c-f) were conducted with matched model groups, while the comparison of CRISPR outcomes (g,h) were performed between unmatched, different groups of models.

Extended Data Fig. 5Dependencies linked to gene expression identified in NextGen vs traditional models.a, Representative distribution of dependency scores for each dependency category. Each gene evaluated by the CRISPR screen was classified into either of these five dependency classes based on the distribution of its Chronos dependency scores across DepMap NextGen models (or organoid models). We used a previously published strategy for this classification25 (also see Methods). b, Correlation of expression and dependency for PROX1 and ERBB2 in the NextGen (left) and traditional (right) models. Elevated expression of PROX1 correlated with enhanced dependency on its own more strongly in the NextGen models (r = −0.462) than in the traditional cell lines (r = −0.182). In contrast, while the traditional cell lines exhibit very strong association (r = −0.530) between the expression and dependency levels of ERBB2, this relationship was much weaker (r = −0.077) in the NextGen models. Here and in e, regression lines with 95% confidence intervals are displayed. c, Increased expression of HNRNPH1 and PROX1 and reduced expression of ENO2 in tumors relative to lineage-matched normal tissues. The expression levels of HNRNPH1, PROX1 and ENO2 in the tumor tissues and corresponding normal tissues were analyzed per lineage in the combined TCGA/TARGET/GTEx dataset downloaded from the Xena browser (https://xenabrowser.net/). n = 9 (biliary tract, normal), 36 (biliary tract, tumor), 1,151 (CNS-brain, normal), 689 (CNS-brain, tumor), 355 (colorectal, normal), 383 (colorectal, tumor), 152 (prostate, normal), and 496 (prostate, tumor). Expression values were plotted for the lineages with tumor-specific upregulation (HNRNPH1 and PROX1) or downregulation (ENO2) of these genes. The centre line and box denote median and 25th to 75th percentile data points, respectively, and whiskers extend up to 1.5 times the interquartile range from box edges. P-values were scored by two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test. d, Reduced expression of ESR1/ERBB2 underlies the absence of expression addiction for these oncogenes in the NextGen breast cancer models. The association between the expression and dependency of two breast cancer oncogenes, ESR1 and ERBB2, was plotted for the NextGen (green circles) and traditional (navy circles) breast cancer models. None of the 14 breast cancer organoids exhibited high (log2[TPM + 1] > 3.4) expression of ESR1, while 11 out of the 51 traditional breast cancer models showed high expression of this oncogene. All the traditional cell lines with strong (Chronos score < −1) ESR1 dependency displayed high expression of ESR1. Similarly, only one out of the 14 NextGen models, and 14 out of the 51 traditional cell lines, exhibited high expression of ERBB2 (log2[TPM + 1] > 7.5) and the majority (10/12) of the traditional cell lines whose screen results exhibit strong ERBB2 dependencies were found to have high ERBB2 expression. Hence, the absence of expression addiction relationship for ESR1 and ERBB2 in the NextGen breast cancer models appears to be attributable, in part, to the reduced expression of these oncogenes in these models as compared to the levels observed in their traditional counterparts. e, ELMO2 paralog dependency in the NextGen (left) vs traditional (right) models. ELMO2 dependency was correlated strongly (r = 0.545) with reduced expression of its paralog ELMO3 in the traditional cell lines, while this relationship was not observed (r = −0.110) in the NextGen models.

# Most reproduced "organoid-specific" cancer dependencies are consistent with culture-medium effects: a genome-wide attribution of the 2026 organoid dependency catalogues

*Technical note / resource. Draft v2r2, 2026-10-30 (revised after independent skeptical review). Analysis code and tables: `src/medium_attribution_v2.py`, `generations/medium_attribution_v2_*.csv` (see release README).*

## Abstract

Two 2026 Nature studies (Neiswender et al., Broad/NextGen; Herranz-Ors et al., Sanger) published genome-wide CRISPR dependency catalogues for patient-derived organoids and nominated organoid-specific dependencies as candidate drug targets. Because organoid media are defined, serum-free formulations — lipid- and nutrient-poor relative to serum or plasma — some of these dependencies may reflect culture medium rather than tumor biology. Neiswender et al. showed this for sterol-synthesis genes in a 1,000-gene minipool; the genome-wide, per-gene decomposition has not been reported. Here we decompose every organoid-vs-2D differential dependency in the DepMap 26Q3 release using organoid-medium models grown adherent (similar formulation family, no dome), dome-vs-adherent contrasts within organoid medium, and an unrelated serum-free lineage (CNS in Tumor Stem Media), with library (Avana vs Humagne-CD), lineage, and dynamic-range adjustment, on development patients with disjoint held-out-patient confirmation. Of 456 differential dependencies, 84–86% are classified medium-consistent under stated rules (75–82% under heteroscedasticity-robust SEs; bootstrap slope for adherent reproduction 0.90, 95% CI 0.82–0.99); one gene (LSM7) meets symmetric nominal criteria for format association and none do at 5% FDR. Among the Broad catalogue's published gains, 47% are medium-consistent overall and 87% of those that replicate under lineage adjustment; of Herranz-Ors et al.'s 18 headline genes, 8 of 16 present replicate — 5 medium-consistent (the SREBP/sterol axis MVD, IDI1, MBTPS1, MBTPS2, PNKP) and 3 unresolved. Dependency losses behave similarly (84% medium-consistent); the curated ribosomal set shows a relative weakening that survives global corrections in both assays, for which depletion kinetics under fewer doublings is a testable but unproven explanation. These are consistency classifications, not causal proof: adherent comparators cover 6 of 9 lineages (38/68 dome models) and mixed formulations. We release the per-gene table, with bootstrap flag frequencies, so any nominated organoid target can be checked before wet-lab investment.

## Introduction

Organoid dependency maps are being used to nominate targets that 2D screens miss. The interpretive risk is that "organoid-specific" conflates three differences from classical DepMap screens: 3D format (Matrigel domes), defined serum-free medium, and the Humagne-CD CRISPR library. Patients' tumors are perfused with plasma containing LDL cholesterol, fatty acids, heme/iron carriers, and Wnt ligands; organoid media supply few of these. A dependency that exists only because the medium lacks LDL may not hold in vivo; add-back experiments can test LDL limitation in cultured models, while transfer to tumors would remain untested.

What is already established, and not claimed here: Neiswender et al. (Nature 2026) ran a paired minipool 2×2 (format × serum), showed SQLE/MSMO1 dependency is medium-driven, identified seven format-associated genes including the integrins ITGB1/ITGAV/ITGA3, and concluded format has at most modest effects under serum-free conditions; the LDLR/SREBP sterol-starvation response is textbook physiology; Wnt-secretion dependency in Wnt-free formulations is expected. What has not been done: a genome-wide, per-gene attribution of the *published catalogues* — how many nominated hits are consistent with medium effects, which named targets are affected, whether dependency losses behave the same way, and how the apparent weakening of core essentials in dome screens should be interpreted. That quantification is the contribution here; our one format-consistent genome-wide hit and the format-leaning unresolved set (which includes ITGB1) are consistent with, not a rediscovery of, the minipool format findings.

## Results

### Design

From DepMap 26Q3 CRISPR screens passing QC we formed, on development patients (a patient-level hold-out sequestered before analysis; calibration, gene filtering, and imputation use development screens only): organoid-medium dome models (n=68) and organoid-medium *adherent* models (n=9) across 9 lineages; FBS-adherent models in the same lineages (n=207); and CNS models in serum-free Tumor Stem Media vs FBS (n=29 vs 60). Per-gene library bias was removed using 22 development FBS models screened with both Avana and Humagne-CD (all Avana screens in this release are FBS, so no cross-medium invariance of the offset is assumed; transfer across FBS models is). For each gene we estimate four lineage-adjusted contrasts: D (dome organoid medium vs FBS 2D), A (adherent organoid medium vs FBS 2D — formulation family without dome; individual formulations differ), F (dome vs adherent within organoid medium), and S (TSM vs FBS in CNS). Hits (D q<0.01, |Δ|≥0.25) are flagged **medium-consistent** (column `medium_attributable` in the released table) when A reproduces ≥50% of D with nominal p<0.05 and a 90% ratio CI excluding 0, and F does not meet the symmetric criteria; **format_candidate** under the corresponding rule for F (same ratio/CI/nominal-p requirements, plus adherent ratio < 0.25 so the effect is not substantially reproduced without the dome); otherwise unresolved. A strict variant requiring genome-wide F q<0.05 is released alongside (`flag_fdr`). Flags are consistency classifications under these rules, not causal identification: the adherent comparators span 6 of 9 lineages and several formulations, and derivation/selection differences between model populations cannot be excluded by lineage adjustment. Analyses on raw Chronos and dynamic-range-normalized scores agree; normalized is primary.

### Most differential dependencies are medium-consistent, in both directions

We find 249 dependency gains and 207 losses. 86% of gains and 84% of losses are medium-consistent; one gene (LSM7) is a format candidate under symmetric nominal criteria and none at 5% FDR (minimum F q ≈ 1.0, so the FDR statement is about detection power, not absence of format biology — 34 hits have same-direction F/D ≥ 0.5). Slopes of A on D are 0.84 (gains) and 0.86 (losses), versus 0.18/0.17 for F. Under HC3 robust SEs the medium-consistent fractions are 82%/75%. Leave-one-out over the 9 adherent models: slope 0.88–0.92, ≥93.5% of flags retained (F refitted per omission). A joint bootstrap (one model resample shared by calibration and analysis, B=150; identity replicate reproduces point flags exactly) gives A-on-D slope 0.90 [95% CI 0.82–0.99]; per-gene flags are less stable than the slope (72% of hits flagged medium-consistent in ≥50% of replicates; released as bootstrap frequencies), so individual flags should be read with their CIs and frequencies, not as binary truth. Restricting to the six lineages with adherent comparators (38 dome models) leaves the pattern intact (slope 0.89, median ratio 0.89, 90% of subset hits with ratio ≥ 0.5). Disjoint held-out patients (25 domes vs 78 reserved-patient FBS controls, no shared baseline) confirm: dev→held-out slope 0.96 (r=0.97), 100% sign concordance among medium-consistent hits, held-out adherent reproduction slope 0.90 (Fig. 1).

Named medium-consistent gains include the sterol pathway (SQLE Δ=−0.83, adherent ratio 1.08; MSMO1 −0.81, 0.68), fatty-acid synthesis (FASN −0.42, 1.00; ACLY −0.42, 0.91), heme synthesis (ALAS1 −0.42; FECH −0.37), and Wnt secretion/reception (FZD5, LGR4, WLS; ratios 0.91–1.07, absent in TSM — consistent with Wnt-free formulations, though this conflicts with the NextGen minipool at these genes and rests on 9 adherent models).

Expression data (condition-mapped Omics TPM, same contrasts) corroborate the sterol axis on an orthogonal data type: mevalonate-pathway expression rises by median Δ +0.36 against a dependency Δ of −0.38 (SQLE expression +0.75 vs dependency −0.83; LDLR expression +0.61; pathway score −0.01 FBS-adherent, +0.18 organoid-medium adherent, +0.44 domes) — the expected sterol-starvation signature. Heme and fatty-acid synthesis expression move oppositely (−0.47, −0.36), so expression supports the sterol mechanism specifically (genome-wide corr(Δdependency, Δexpression) ≈ 0).

A specificity control comes from plasma-like medium. In Rossiter et al.'s genome-wide K562 screens (RPMI vs human plasma-like medium, both with dialyzed serum — so not an LDL-removal experiment), the HPLM−RPMI shift is genome-wide near-orthogonal to our organoid contrast (r = 0.04), and SQLE is *relatively less* essential in HPLM (Δ +0.44, differential Z +3.8) versus the strongest gain in serum-free organoid medium. Genes relatively more essential in RPMI (Z>3) are enriched for our medium-consistent gains (odds ratio 4.4, prevalence ratio 4.2, Fisher p = 0.007) — medium-associated dependencies appear bidirectional and partly shared: several dependencies strongest in serum-free organoid medium are weaker in physiological than in conventional formulation in this independent system — cross-system concordance, not a shared-mechanism demonstration. (Single genome-wide line; dialyzed serum in both arms.)

### Audit of the published catalogues

Against the Broad study's published organoids-vs-2D table (Mann-Whitney, unadjusted): of 285 published gains (FDR<0.05, Δ<−0.25), 156 (55%) replicate as lineage-adjusted hits on development patients. Medium-consistent are 135 — 47% of the published list, 87% of the replicating subset — with 20 unresolved, 1 format candidate (LSM7), and 129 not reproduced under lineage adjustment (attribution unestablished, not evidence of biology). The 17 strictest gains (FDR<0.01, Δ<−0.5) are 16 medium-consistent, 1 unresolved. Published losses (n=252): 52% medium-consistent overall, 86% of the 153 replicating.

Against Herranz-Ors et al.: their calls are prevalent within their own assay (in their BAGEL binary matrix, collapsing dual-library profiles within model, exclusive genes are depletion-called in a median 80% of organoids and headline genes in 70%; this measures call prevalence, not robustness to threshold choice, which binary calls cannot assess) — the open question is attribution. Of 97 organoid-exclusive genes (93 in the Broad table), 19 replicate as Broad differential hits (14 gains, 5 losses): 14 medium-consistent, 5 unresolved. Of the headline 18 (16 in-table), 8 replicate, all gains: 5 medium-consistent (MVD, IDI1, MBTPS1, MBTPS2, PNKP — the first four are the SREBP/sterol axis; 5/16 in-table, 5/8 of replicating) and 3 unresolved (SCAP, ratio 0.87, fails nominal adherent significance p=0.057; DDX3X and ITGB1, ratios ≤0.35). ITGB1's unresolved, format-leaning status here is consistent with Neiswender et al.'s minipool format finding for integrins.

### Relative ribosomal weakening in organoid screens: depletion kinetics is a testable explanation, not an established one

The strongest individual losses are spliceosome/ribosome subunits (top Δ up to +1.2 raw Chronos). With curated BAGEL reference sets (spliceosome n=35, ribosomal n=38), Broad median Δ is +0.016 (spliceosome) and +0.172 (ribosomal) against +0.031 for the essential-set baseline: weakening is concentrated in subsets of subunits (13/38 ribosomal and 5/35 spliceosome genes are medium-consistent losses), with ribosomal the only complex showing a clear whole-set shift (a small hand-picked panel median reported in our earlier internal analysis, +0.90, overstates the complex-wide effect and is not used). In Broad data the shift is not a whole-screen scale change *as visible after Chronos' per-screen rescaling* (median common-essential Chronos ratio dome/FBS = 1.00; dome screens run longer, 24 vs 21 days), and it reproduces in adherent organoid medium (ribosomal median A +0.20, within-family format contrast −0.01) — but Chronos rescaling also means Broad data cannot speak to global dynamics directly. In Sanger's assay (organoid table 6 LFC vs 930 2D lines), reference-essential depth is 0.63× in organoids; because the two matrices are processed differently (nonessential medians also differ, −0.002 vs +0.121), we treat LFC magnitudes as secondary. On processing-robust within-model percentiles, ribosomal genes are relatively weaker in Sanger organoids (0.021 vs 0.011) while spliceosome genes are not (0.018 vs 0.027); depth-scaled LFC agrees for ribosomal (1.25 vs 1.57 ×depth). Fewer accumulated doublings with slow depletion of long-lived complexes would produce exactly this pattern, but cumulative doublings are recorded for only 1 of 1,241 Broad screens, so the mechanism is untested here and alternatives (e.g. medium-driven turnover changes) remain open. Neither 2026 catalogue reports or adjusts for the weakening; absolute-threshold "organoid-specific essential" calls are exposed to it in both directions (cf. the 5 Herranz-Ors exclusives that are losses in Broad data). As a cross-system control, the mevalonate gain is visible within Sanger's assay (percentile 0.099 in organoids vs 0.394 in Sanger 2D lines).

## Discussion

For target nomination the practical rule is: an organoid-specific dependency in a nutrient-synthesis pathway (sterol, fatty-acid, heme) should be treated as medium-consistent until tested under repletion, because plasma supplies the end products in vivo. The sterol-axis genes on Herranz-Ors et al.'s headline list (MVD, IDI1, MBTPS1/2, SCAP) are exactly this case. Conversely, genes that do not reproduce in adherent organoid medium (DDX3X, ITGB1 among headline genes; COASY, LSM7, UTP4 among Broad published gains) are the better follow-up candidates — with ITGB1 independently format-associated in the NextGen minipool. Dependency losses deserve symmetric caution: weaker ribosomal/spliceosomal dependency in organoid screens should not be read as reduced target relevance until doublings-resolved data exist.

Limitations. (1) Identification: medium consistency is established by reproduction across *different model populations* sharing a formulation family; adherent comparators cover 6/9 lineages and 38/68 domes have same-lineage comparators, formulations are not identical across arms, and derivation/selection differences are not excluded. Causal medium attribution requires perturbation (add-back) experiments. (2) Uncertainty: per-gene flags are materially less stable than the aggregate slopes (bootstrap frequencies released; HC3 fractions 75–82%); the library offset rests on 22 development dual-library models, and the screen-filtered Humagne-only sensitivity has 7 FBS controls (r=0.78 with the main estimate, slope 0.83 — consistent but inconclusive alone). (3) Format power: with 9 adherent models the F contrast detects nothing at 5% FDR; one gene passes symmetric nominal criteria. (4) Sanger analyses use published LFC tables with different processing across matrices; percentile-based results are primary. (5) CPD/doubling data are essentially absent from 26Q3, so deliverable dynamics corrections are limited to dynamic-range normalization and screen days.

Decisive tests. (1) LDL/cholesterol add-back in organoid-medium models should return the mevalonate dependency score toward the FBS baseline and restore LDLR dependency. (2) Statin/SQLE-inhibitor potency should shift ≥5-fold between matched FBS and defined medium, while ITGB1-class candidates should not respond to LDL. (3) Doubling-recorded screens should test whether ribosomal Chronos recovers per doubling. A concrete protocol for (1–2) with pre-agreed falsification criteria accompanies this note.

item.text:
The searches have reached practical saturation for the central claim: successive searches for catalogue reanalyses, medium-attribution fractions, correction methods, and critical citations are returning known papers or unrelated work. The remaining new leads concern individual pathways or drug responses. No verified source reports the requested genome-wide medium-attribution fractions for the two catalogues.

The manuscript nevertheless needs narrower wording: its strongest defensible contribution is a catalogue-wide **medium-consistency classification**, and it should credit the original genome-wide format analyses.

Despite advances in precision oncology, effective personalized treatments are still lacking for most patients with cancer1. The Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap) accelerates this field by systematically identifying cancer vulnerabilities in diverse preclinical models. Data from over 1,300 cell lines have led to the discovery of new therapeutic strategies across multiple tumour types2. However, mapping cancer vulnerabilities using traditional cell lines has limitations, including insufficient cancer subtype representation and the impact of culture conditions on perturbation responses. Here we perform 147 genome-scale CRISPR screens and multi-omic characterizations of next-generation (NextGen) cancer models (organoids and spheroids) across 10 cancer types. This strategy enables the expansion of DepMap to cover new genomic and molecular subtypes and to identify new biomarker-associated vulnerabilities. These new models also preserve transcriptional programs that are silenced in traditional cell lines and facilitate the discovery of specific gene dependencies associated with these programs. Comparisons of traditional and NextGen cancer models enable further identification of distinct effects of growth format and culture medium on gene essentiality. The integrated dataset combines data from both model types to offer a valuable, expansive resource for exploring cancer vulnerabilities and is accessible via the DepMap portal.

We collected 314 NextGen models comprising 237 carcinoma organoids and 77 central nervous system (CNS) tumour spheroids8–11 (Fig. 1a,b and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b) and generated WGS and RNA-seq profiles from 291 and 309 models, respectively. WGS confirmed expected recurrent genomic alterations, including the following changes: TP53 and APC mutations and chromosome 18q loss in colorectal models; TERT promoter mutations in CNS models; and TP53 and KRAS mutations and chromosome 9p loss in pancreas models (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). NextGen models also captured mutations not represented in traditional models, such as NRAS in colorectal cancer (4.4% prevalence)12 and ESR1 in breast cancer (7% prevalence)12, and expanded prostate cancer representation with previously underrepresented alterations (SPOP, RB1, APC and CTNNB1; Fig. 1c,d and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b).Fig. 1Multiomics and functional profiling of NextGen cancer models.a, Illustration of NextGen model profiling in DepMap. The combination of multiomic characterization and functional genomic profiling at DepMap is extended to NextGen models. The colour code for individual cancer lineages shown here is used in b–e. b, Lineage composition of the NextGen models profiled for each of the assay types. c, Comparison of alteration frequencies per lineage for selected genes across TCGA tumours, NextGen models and traditional cell lines. The intensity of the colour represents the proportion of tumours or models with the indicated genomic alteration. Red frames indicate that values are sourced from publications describing a similar tumour dataset12,58–60 but not from the same TCGA dataset13 used in other parts of this study. d, Oncoprint of NextGen models with mutations and CN alterations of driver genes that were not represented in the traditional DepMap models of their respective lineages. e, Celligner embedding of gene expression for tumour samples and NextGen cancer models. f, Lineage prediction based on nearest neighbour (NN) tumour samples in Celligner. Oeso–stm, oesophagus–stomach. For each of the NextGen and traditional models, the lineages of the 25 nearest neighbour tumour samples (y axis) were plotted for each of the annotated lineages of the models (x axis). g, Distributions of mean dependency log fold changes (naive gene effect) of nonessential (blue) and common essential (maroon) genes. h,i, Illustration of data integration steps across screens using Chronos (h) with a plot of Avana and Humagne data shown for pre-Chronos and post-Chronos processing (i). Schematic in a created in BioRender; Vazquez, F. https://biorender.com/fd5u98k (2026).Source data

We performed genome-scale CRISPR screens on 147 NextGen models using the Humagne enAsCas12a single-guide RNA (sgRNA) library21 (Extended Data Fig. 3). Screen quality was comparable between NextGen models and traditional cell lines screened using spCas9 (n = 1,351) or enAsCas12a (n = 36) sgRNA libraries. Moreover, both showed clear separation of non-essential and essential sgRNA score distributions and similar receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) and null-normalized mean difference (NNMD) scores (Fig. 1g and Extended Data Fig. 4a,b).

CNS models were screened as spheroids or on matrix-coated plates (termed ‘coat’ hereafter) and organoids were screened in Matrigel domes or in coat conditions, all in serum-free media (Supplementary Table 1). Gene expression and essentiality profiles were nearly identical across CNS growth formats (Pearson’s r = 0.996 and 0.990, respectively), and organoid gene dependencies also strongly agreed between the two conditions (r = 0.984; Extended Data Fig. 4c–h). These results suggest that growth format does not significantly affect CRISPR screen outcomes under serum-free conditions. This finding is in contrast to a previous study that used serum-containing media22—a discrepancy that may be attributable to differences in medium composition and the comparison strategy used. All models were profiled for WGS, RNA-seq and CRISPR under identical conditions.

Expression addiction, in which gene essentiality correlates with increased levels of its own expression (common for oncogenes and lineage-defining transcription factors23,25–27), was identified for 51 strong dependencies (r < −0.3, q < 0.005). These included 14 oncogenes (P = 6.21 × 10−10, one-sided Fisher’s exact test) and 21 transcription factors (P = 3.09 × 10−14; Fig. 2a,b and Supplementary Table 2). Among these were HNRNPH1 and PROX1, both implicated in brain tumours28,29 (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 5b). The dependency–expression correlation was stronger for both genes in NextGen models, and both displayed increased expression in brain tumours relative to normal tissue (Extended Data Fig. 5c). HNRNPH1 also exhibited elevated expression in biliary tract cancers, as did PROX1 in colorectal cancers, which may represent tumour-specific vulnerabilities.Fig. 2Biomarker-associated vulnerabilities identified in NextGen models.a–c, Expression addiction. Notably, expression addictions for certain lineage-specific oncogenes were found only in traditional cell lines. ESR1 addiction, which is central to oestrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer, was absent in NextGen models (r = 0.033 for NextGen versus r = –0.637 for traditional; Fig. 2c). This result is consistent with insufficient ESR1 expression in breast organoids (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 5d) and previous reports of its progressive loss in organoid culture30,31. Similarly, ERBB2 addiction was absent in organoids, with only 3 out of 146 NextGen models expressing ERBB2 at levels to cause its dependency (log2[transcripts per million (TPM) + 1] > 7.5; Extended Data Fig. 5b,d). These findings indicate that there are differences between NextGen and traditional models in their dependencies on oncogenes.

Paralogue dependencies arise when the loss of a gene increases reliance on its paralogue26,32,33. We evaluated all paralogue pairs with >25% identity and identified 106 strong dependencies linked to reduced paralogue expression (r > 0.3, q < 0.005; Fig. 2d and Supplementary Table 2). Several were stronger in NextGen models, including ENO1 dependency linked to low ENO2 expression, than in traditional models (r = 0.455 versus r = 0.233, respectively; Fig. 2e). ENO2, a neuron-specific enolase34, showed lineage-appropriate expression only in NextGen models (Fig. 2e). Its reduced expression in colorectal and prostate cancers relative to normal tissue (Extended Data Fig. 5c) suggests that ENO1 inhibition could selectively target these tumours. Previous work has also linked ENO1 CN deletion to ENO2 dependency in glioblastoma (GBM)35, which indicates that there is mutual paralogue dependency. Conversely, some relationships were weaker in NextGen models. These included ELMO2 dependency tied to low ELMO3 expression (r = –0.110 (NextGen) versus r = 0.545 (traditional); Extended Data Fig. 5e), which suggests that there are different requirements for ELMO2-mediated cytoskeletal rearrangement across model types.

We next explored transcriptional differences between NextGen and traditional models, with the aim of gaining insight into distinct dependency profiles. To that end, we characterized their differentially activated biological programs using 41 gene expression meta-programs (MPs), as identified in a previous study37. These MPs represent recurrent gene expression modules that account for intratumour heterogeneity (Fig. 3a) and largely reflect environmentally driven gene expression changes. We therefore reasoned that the distinct culture conditions of NextGen and traditional models would lead to differential MP activation. To evaluate this hypothesis, we quantified MP activity by comparing NextGen (n = 76) and traditional (n = 97) CNS models and organoids (n = 229) with lineage-matched traditional cell lines (n = 451), and each organoid lineage against its traditional counterpart. Substantial variations in MP activity were observed between NextGen and traditional CNS models and between organoids and traditional cell lines (Fig. 3a). Accordingly, we generated a focused enAsCas12a sgRNA minipool library targeting 250 genes from 9 core functional classes (5 related to adhesion–cytoskeleton, 1 for lipid metabolism and an additional 3 from the 3D versus 2D dependency comparison; Fig. 5c, Extended Data Fig. 9a and Supplementary Table 3). Viability screens using this library were conducted across seven models, testing combinations of growth format (2D plastic or 3D Matrigel dome) and medium type (serum-containing RPMI–FBS or serum-free OPAC) for a total of 18 screens (Extended Data Fig. 9b).

To validate these findings, we knocked out ITB1, ITGAV, MSMO1 or SQLE in KP3 and HS766T pancreas models under 2D plastic (with RPMI–FBS) and 3D dome (with RPMI–FBS or OPAC) cultures. Cholesterol biosynthesis gene dependencies (MSMO1 and SQLE) varied by medium, whereas integrin subunit dependencies (ITGAV and ITGB1) were sensitive to growth format (Fig. 5h and Extended Data Fig. 10a). Immunofluorescence analyses confirmed that integrin β1 (encoded by ITGB1) colocalized with FAK in 3D but not 2D cultures, whereas integrin αV (encoded by ITGAV) showed enhanced FAK colocalization in 2D relative to 3D cultures, which was partially due to reduced cell surface expression in 3D (Fig. 5i and Extended Data Fig. 10b–e). These findings align with their differential roles in cell–ECM interactions across different growth formats55.

Our data also revealed that oncogenic signalling roles differ significantly between model types. WNT signalling is required for organoids with a PDAC-classical/MUC program but is largely dispensable in traditional models (Fig. 4). By contrast, dependencies on ESR1 and ERBB2 were exclusive to traditional cell lines (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 5b,d), which probably stem from reduced expression of these oncogenes in the organoids (Extended Data Fig. 5d) owing to composition differences in the media. Together, these findings demonstrate that multiple oncogenic signalling pathways are highly context-dependent, which reinforces the fact that cellular microenvironments substantially shape requirements for these pathways56,57.

RNA-seq for all the DepMap NextGen models was conducted at the Broad Institute Genomics Platform. In brief, poly-A RNAs were captured with oligo-dT beads, from which libraries (450–550 bp insert size) were prepared using a strand-specific Illumina TruSeq library preparation protocol. These libraries were sequenced to 100 million paired reads on either an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 or NovaSeq X system, with the use of 151 bp paired-end reads. The FASTQ files from sequencing were processed using the DRAGEN RNA-seq pipeline to create BAM files.

After initial expansion and collection of viable stocks and pellets (used for fingerprinting and omics profiling; Extended Data Fig. 3), the organoids were tested for blasticidin sensitivity to identify the minimal concentration of blasticidin that gives less than 1% viability of uninfected cells in 10–14 days. Fourteen organoid models were screened as adherent cultures on Matrigel-coated plates, whereas the rest of the organoids were screened in 3D Matrigel dome cultures. To select the culture conditions for organoid screens, each of the organoid models was subjected to a growth format assay by seeding 50,000 cells into a well of a 24-well non-tissue-culture-treated plate (Corning, 351147) either as a Matrigel dome (75% Matrigel, 50 μl per dome) or on top of a Matrigel coat, referred to as either dome or coat format, respectively. The coated wells were prepared by first adding 1% Matrigel in ice-cold PBS to 50% of the standard filling volume of the well and allowing it to solidify by incubating overnight at 37 °C. Before cell plating, the PBS–Matrigel mixture was aspirated, leaving the Matrigel coat behind, and the cell suspension was added on top of the coat. The growth of cells in the dome and coat formats was compared after 1 week of culture via a viability assay with CellTiter-Glo 3D (3D CTG; Promega, G9683). Models with at least 30% viability on coat relative to dome format were propagated and screened in the coat format. This process enabled us to screen these models in a similar manner to traditional adherent cell lines, but with a thin layer of matrix support, thus decreasing the amount of required Matrigel by approximately tenfold.

For the NextGen CNS tumour models and organoids, the gene dependency profiles were compared between the two different culture conditions used for each of these model groups. Specifically, for the NextGen CNS models, the dependency scores between spheroid culture (n = 14) and coat culture (n = 25) and for organoids, and the dependency scores between Matrigel dome culture (n = 55) and coat culture (n = 14) were compared for every gene assessed in the CRISPR screen of these models (n = 18,159) using two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests (Extended Data Fig. 4h). For the organoids in Matrigel dome cultures, only the models from lineages that have corresponding coat-cultured models (ampulla of Vater, colorectal, oesophagus–stomach, ovary, prostate and uterus) were included in this comparison.

The classification of dependency profiles (Extended Data Fig. 5a) was conducted primarily based on a published strategy25 using the entire set of the NextGen (n = 147) and organoid (n = 108) models. First, we identified a negative control set of non-expressed genes per model as having a log2[TPM + 1] expression value of less than 0.2. We then inferred the probability that the score represents a true dependency by using an expectation–maximization step until convergence independently in each screen or model. The dependent distribution was derived from the list of essential genes, which was generated from the intersection of previously published lists of essential genes70,71. The null distribution was determined from non-expressed gene scores for the respective model if the expression data were available, or otherwise from the non-essential gene list inferred from a published study70.

To find dependencies that are associated with oncogene GOF or TSG LOF, we first identified models with oncogene GOF as either harbouring a hotspot mutation or CN gain (log2[relative to ploidy + 1] > 3) of the oncogene, and TSG LOF as either having a damaging mutation or CN loss (log2[relative to ploidy + 1] < 0.25) of the TSG for all the oncogenes and TSGs listed in OncoKB1 (https://www.oncokb.org/). We selected 6 oncogenes and 13 TSGs that had at least 1 model of hotspot mutation and 5 or more models of relevant alteration among the NextGen models with CRISPR screen profiles (n = 147). For each of these oncogenes and TSGs, we assessed whether any of the strong dependencies were significantly enriched in the NextGen models with the respective cancer gene alteration (‘altered’) compared with the rest of these models (‘unaltered’) using two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests with a threshold of q < 0.05 (Fig. 2f).

To examine whether the increased reliance on SCD of oesophageal adenocarcinoma organoids with KRAS CN amplification, identified via CRISPR screens, can be reproduced with pharmacological SCD inhibition, we tested two chemical inhibitors of SCD: A939572 and CAY-10566. Specifically, we tested four oesophageal adenocarcinoma models, two with KRAS CN amplification (CCLFUPGI0012T and CCLFUPGI0030T) and two with neutral KRAS CN (CCLFUPGI0022T and HCMSANG0300C15). On day 0, for each of these four models, 10,000 cells per well were seeded into 120 wells of 96-well ULA plates (Revvity, 6055802) in a slurry culture with 100 μl of 5% Matrigel–OPAC per well. One of the following compounds was added to the culture at the same time as seeding using a D500e Digital Dispenser (Tecan Life Sciences): A939572, CAY-10566 and bortezomib. For each of these compounds, nine different doses with serial dilutions (2 nM to 10 μM, 2.9-fold dilution between the neighbouring doses) and DMSO control were tested in quadruplicate. On day 3, 50 μl fresh medium containing the corresponding concentration of the compounds was added to the culture.

To analyse gene expression and associated dependencies in the NextGen GBM models, the transcriptional landscape of GBM models was visualized in a 2D UMAP using Celligner embedding (Fig. 3b). The cohort included 55 traditional and 70 NextGen GBM models, alongside 189 tumour samples from the TCGA-plus and Met500 GBM cohort. Two clusters were identified visually on the UMAP plot on the basis of distinct groupings of data points. Differential gene expression analysis was conducted to compare the transcriptional profiles of the clusters by computing log2 fold changes to quantify expression differences and performing two-tailed Student’s t-tests to assess significance for each gene. Significance was determined using adjusted P values (q values), with thresholds applied at q < 0.001 and |log2[fold change]| > 1 (Fig. 3c).

Plates (both time = 0 and treated plates) were stained, fixed, imaged and analysed according to the Dye Drop or Deep Dye Drop protocols43. In brief, for Dye Drop, cells were stained with Hoechst 33342 (1:5,000, Thermo Fisher, 62249) and LIVE/DEAD far red fluorescent dye (LDR, 1:2,000, Thermo Fisher, L10120), prepared in a 10% solution of OptiPrep (Sigma, D1556) in PBS to displace the growth medium, for 30 min at RT. Cells were then fixed with 4% formaldehyde, prepared in 20% OptiPrep (a denser solution to displace the stain solution and media column), for 30 min at RT. Fix, stain and medium were aspirated and 80 µl PBS was added per well. Plates were then sealed and stored at 4 °C until image acquisition. For Deep Dye Drop, cells were stained with LDR and pulsed with EdU (Lumiprobe, 30540) in a 10% solution of OptiPrep in PBS for 1 h before fixation with 4% formaldehyde, prepared in 20% OptiPrep for 30 min. Wells were aspirated and cells were then permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 (Sigma, T8787) in 10% OptiPrep for 20 min at RT, and EdU was then labelled with cy3-azide (Lumiprobe, C1030) by Click chemistry in 20% OptiPrep for 30 min at RT. Following aspiration, cells were blocked in Odyssey buffer (LI-COR Biosciences, 927-40150) for 1 h at RT, and then stained with anti-phospho histone H3 Alexa 488 (pH3, 1:2,000, Cell Signaling Technologies, 3465S) and Hoechst 33342 (1:5,000) overnight at 4 °C. Cells were washed once with PBST, twice with PBS and sealed for storage at 4 °C until image acquisition. All wash steps were performed with an EL406 washer equipped with a 96-channel head (Biotek).

The viability effect (10 days after sgRNA transduction) of CRISPR-mediated knockout of ITGB1, ITGAV, MSMO1 and SQLE (Fig. 5h and Extended Data Fig. 10a) was assessed using CTG cell viability assays. Specifically, KP3 and HS766T pancreatic cancer cells, both of which were engineered to express enAsCas12a, were infected with several different types of sgRNA-expressing lentivirus on day 0, which included CRISPR cutting controls (sgCh2 and sgAAVS1), sgRNAs targeting common essential genes (sgPOLR2D, sgSF3B1 and sgKIF11) and sgRNAs against the experimental genes (sgITGB1, sgITGAV, sgMSMO1 and sgSQLE). The infected cells were selected with 2 μg ml–1 puromycin between day 1 and day 3. On day 3, cells were trypsinized, counted and reseeded without puromycin. For the 2D monolayer culture on a plastic plate (or plastic culture), cells were seeded at 2,000 cells per well in 100 µl RPMI medium with 10% FBS onto an opaque 96-well plate (Corning, 3903). For the 3D Matrigel dome culture (or dome culture), 10,000 cells were resuspended with 50 μl Matrigel and plated as a dome onto a 12-well plate, which was subsequently incubated (Corning, 356231) at 37 °C for 30 min to allow the Matrigel to solidify. The Matrigel dome was then covered with 1,200 μl per well of either the RPMI medium with 10% FBS or the 1:1 OPAC medium before further incubation. The medium was replaced every 3 days until day 10. Puromycin (2 μg ml–1) was added back to the culture at the first medium replacement.

For immunostaining of cells grown in either plastic culture or the dome culture conditions, cells were propagated on a Nunc 8-Well Lab-Tek chamber slide (Thermo Fisher, 177402). For plastic culture, the slide was first incubated with 100 μg ml–1 collagen I (Corning, 354236) and 20 μg ml−1 laminin (SouthernBiotech, 1415-01) for 60 min at 37 °C. Subsequently, 20,000 cells were seeded with 200 μl RPMI with 10% FBS per well. For dome culture, 30,000 cells were resuspended with 30 μl Matrigel and placed as a dome at the centre of a well of an 8-well chamber slide. After incubating at 37 °C for 30 min to solidify Matrigel, 200 μl RPMI with 10% FBS was added to the well before further incubation. Fixation and staining were performed essentially as previously described57. In brief, after 3–5 days of culture, cells were washed twice with PBS before fixation. Plastic-cultured cells were fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 20 min at RT. Dome-cultured cells were fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde and 0.2% glutaraldehyde in PBS for 20 min at RT, washed twice with PBS and incubated with 0.2% sodium borohydride for 30 min at 4 °C for the quenching of glutaraldehyde. For both plastic and dome cultures, this fixation procedure was followed by two washes with PBS and two rounds of incubations with 0.1 M glycine in PBS at RT for 10 min for the quenching of paraformaldehyde. After permeabilizing the cells with 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS for 5 min on ice, the slides were incubated with IF buffer (0.1% BSA, 0.2% Triton-X, 0.05% Tween-20 and 0.05% NaN3 in PBS + 10% normal goat serum (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 005-000-121)) for 1 h at RT for blocking. For dome culture, slides were additionally incubated with M.O.M. blocking reagent (Vector Laboratories, MKB-2213-1) for 1 h at RT to reduce endogenous mouse IgG staining of Matrigel. Subsequently, the slides were incubated with primary antibody diluted in IF buffer overnight at RT. After washing with TBS-T (0.05% Tween-20 in TBS) 3 times for 10 min each at RT, slides were incubated with secondary antibody diluted in IF buffer for 1 h at RT. This was followed by washing with PBS-T 4 times for 10 min each at RT and then the slides were incubated with PBS containing 1 μg ml–1 4′6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI; MilliporeSigma, D9452) and Phalloidin-iFluor 647 conjugate (Cayman Chemical, 20555; 1:1,000 dilution) for 30 min at RT for nuclear counterstaining and enhancement of F-actin staining, respectively. For post-fixation, slides were incubated with 1% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 5 min at RT, washed with PBS and incubated with 0.1 M glycine in PBS at RT for 5 min. Finally, cover glasses (no. 1.5) were mounted on the slides with ProLong Gold Antifade mountant (Thermo Fisher, P36930). The following primary and secondary antibodies were used for the staining: anti-FAK (MilliporeSigma, 05-537 (4.47, mouse); 1:200 dilution); anti-FAK (MilliporeSigma, 06-543 (rabbit); 1:200); anti-integrin β1 (BD Pharmingen, 556048 (HUTS-21); 1:50); anti-integrin αV (MilliporeSigma, AB1930; 1:500); goat anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher, A-11001; 1:500); goat anti-rabbit IgG secondary antibody Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher, A-11008; 1:500); goat anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody Alexa Fluor 568 (Thermo Fisher, A-11004; 1:500); and goat anti-rabbit IgG secondary antibody, Alexa Fluor 568 (Thermo Fisher, A-11011; 1:500).

Extended Data Fig. 4Comparison of gene expression and CRISPR screen outcomes between 2D and 3D cultures.a,b, CRISPR screen QC metrics. In a, ROC-AUC (Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve) scores for common essential (positive controls; defined as the intersection of essential genes in Hart et al.70 and Blomen et al.71) and nonessential (negative controls; defined by Hart et al.70) controls were calculated using the naïve gene effect scores and plotted for all the DepMap CRISPR screens. In b, NNMD (Null-Normalized Median Difference) score between the common essential and nonessential controls was calculated for each screen. The screens evaluated here included Cas9 traditional model screens (n = 1,351), enAsCas12a traditional model screens (n = 36), enAsCas12a NextGen organoid screens (n = 108), and enCas12a NextGen CNS model screens (n = 39). For both metrics, scores from the NextGen models were comparable to those from the Cas9 traditional model screens and enAsCas12a traditional model screens. The centre (for consistency with the main text) line and box denote median and 25th to 75th percentile data points, respectively, and whiskers extend up to 1.5 times the interquartile range from box edges. c,d, Clustering of samples from NextGen CNS tumor models in 3D spheroid culture and 2D adherent culture on Matrigel-coated plates (“coat” culture) by the correlation of gene expression. Nine NextGen CNS tumor spheroid models were either maintained in the spheroid culture or propagated in the coat culture for > 4 weeks. In c, gene expression profiles of these 18 samples (9 models x 2 conditions) were compared and clustered using the correlation of expression across top 10% highly variable genes (n = 1,919). These samples were primarily clustered by cell identity, but not by the culture conditions. The distributions of correlation between two different samples were also plotted (d), exhibiting the high degree of correlation (r > 0.8) between two samples with different conditions (spheroid and adherent cultures) of the same model. P-values were calculated with two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test. n = 9 (same model under coat and spheroid culture conditions), 72 (different models under different culture conditions), 36 (different models both in coat cultures), and 36 (different models both in spheroid cultures). e,f, High concordance of gene expression between spheroid and coat cultures of the NextGen CNS models. The mean expression levels in the nine spheroid culture samples (x-axis) and the nine coat culture samples (y-axis) were plotted for all the genes (n = 19,193), which exhibited a very high degree of concordance (r = 0.996) between these two culture conditions (e). The difference in the mean expression levels (x-axis) and the statistical significance of the difference (by a two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test; y-axis) were also plotted (f). The false discovery rate (FDR; q) was 1 for all the genes, indicating that none of the genes exhibited statistically significant differences. g,h Concordance of Chronos dependency scores between 3D culture and 2D coat culture. The mean dependency scores of each gene in the NextGen CNS models screened under 3D spheroid cultures (n = 14; x-axis) and in the NextGen CNS models screened under adherent cultures on laminin- or Matrigel-coated plates (“coat” cultures; n = 25; y-axis) were plotted (g, left). Similarly, the mean dependency scores of genes in the organoid models screened under 3D Matrigel dome cultures (n = 55; x-axis) and in the organoid models screened under coat cultures (n = 14; y-axis) were plotted (g, right). For the organoids in Matrigel dome cultures, only the models from lineages that have corresponding coat-cultured models (ampulla of vator, colorectal, oeso-stm, ovary, prostate and uterus) were included in this comparison. In both cases, a high degree of concordance was observed between the two different conditions of culture (r = 0.990 and 0.984 for CNS models and organoids, respectively). The difference in the mean dependency scores between the spheroid and coat culture of the CNS models (h, left) and between the dome and coat cultures of the organoid models (h, right) (x-axis) and the significance of the difference (y-axis; by a two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test) were also plotted. In both cases, none of the genes exhibited a statistically significant difference of the mean dependency scores between two different culture conditions (q = 1 for all the genes [CNS]; q > 0.71 for all the genes [organoids]). Note that gene expression comparison between spheroid and coat cultures of the NextGen CNS models (c-f) were conducted with matched model groups, while the comparison of CRISPR outcomes (g,h) were performed between unmatched, different groups of models.

Extended Data Fig. 5Dependencies linked to gene expression identified in NextGen vs traditional models.a, Representative distribution of dependency scores for each dependency category. Each gene evaluated by the CRISPR screen was classified into either of these five dependency classes based on the distribution of its Chronos dependency scores across DepMap NextGen models (or organoid models). We used a previously published strategy for this classification25 (also see Methods). b, Correlation of expression and dependency for PROX1 and ERBB2 in the NextGen (left) and traditional (right) models. Elevated expression of PROX1 correlated with enhanced dependency on its own more strongly in the NextGen models (r = −0.462) than in the traditional cell lines (r = −0.182). In contrast, while the traditional cell lines exhibit very strong association (r = −0.530) between the expression and dependency levels of ERBB2, this relationship was much weaker (r = −0.077) in the NextGen models. Here and in e, regression lines with 95% confidence intervals are displayed. c, Increased expression of HNRNPH1 and PROX1 and reduced expression of ENO2 in tumors relative to lineage-matched normal tissues. The expression levels of HNRNPH1, PROX1 and ENO2 in the tumor tissues and corresponding normal tissues were analyzed per lineage in the combined TCGA/TARGET/GTEx dataset downloaded from the Xena browser (https://xenabrowser.net/). n = 9 (biliary tract, normal), 36 (biliary tract, tumor), 1,151 (CNS-brain, normal), 689 (CNS-brain, tumor), 355 (colorectal, normal), 383 (colorectal, tumor), 152 (prostate, normal), and 496 (prostate, tumor). Expression values were plotted for the lineages with tumor-specific upregulation (HNRNPH1 and PROX1) or downregulation (ENO2) of these genes. The centre line and box denote median and 25th to 75th percentile data points, respectively, and whiskers extend up to 1.5 times the interquartile range from box edges. P-values were scored by two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test. d, Reduced expression of ESR1/ERBB2 underlies the absence of expression addiction for these oncogenes in the NextGen breast cancer models. The association between the expression and dependency of two breast cancer oncogenes, ESR1 and ERBB2, was plotted for the NextGen (green circles) and traditional (navy circles) breast cancer models. None of the 14 breast cancer organoids exhibited high (log2[TPM + 1] > 3.4) expression of ESR1, while 11 out of the 51 traditional breast cancer models showed high expression of this oncogene. All the traditional cell lines with strong (Chronos score < −1) ESR1 dependency displayed high expression of ESR1. Similarly, only one out of the 14 NextGen models, and 14 out of the 51 traditional cell lines, exhibited high expression of ERBB2 (log2[TPM + 1] > 7.5) and the majority (10/12) of the traditional cell lines whose screen results exhibit strong ERBB2 dependencies were found to have high ERBB2 expression. Hence, the absence of expression addiction relationship for ESR1 and ERBB2 in the NextGen breast cancer models appears to be attributable, in part, to the reduced expression of these oncogenes in these models as compared to the levels observed in their traditional counterparts. e, ELMO2 paralog dependency in the NextGen (left) vs traditional (right) models. ELMO2 dependency was correlated strongly (r = 0.545) with reduced expression of its paralog ELMO3 in the traditional cell lines, while this relationship was not observed (r = −0.110) in the NextGen models.

The association between the expression and dependency of two breast cancer oncogenes, ESR1 and ERBB2, was plotted for the NextGen (green circles) and traditional (navy circles) breast cancer models. None of the 14 breast cancer organoids exhibited high (log2[TPM + 1] > 3.4) expression of ESR1, while 11 out of the 51 traditional breast cancer models showed high expression of this oncogene. All the traditional cell lines with strong (Chronos score < −1) ESR1 dependency displayed high expression of ESR1. Similarly, only one out of the 14 NextGen models, and 14 out of the 51 traditional cell lines, exhibited high expression of ERBB2 (log2[TPM + 1] > 7.5) and the majority (10/12) of the traditional cell lines whose screen results exhibit strong ERBB2 dependencies were found to have high ERBB2 expression. Hence, the absence of expression addiction relationship for ESR1 and ERBB2 in the NextGen breast cancer models appears to be attributable, in part, to the reduced expression of these oncogenes in these models as compared to the levels observed in their traditional counterparts. e, ELMO2 paralog dependency in the NextGen (left) vs traditional (right) models. ELMO2 dependency was correlated strongly (r = 0.545) with reduced expression of its paralog ELMO3 in the traditional cell lines, while this relationship was not observed (r = −0.110) in the NextGen models.

Raw sequencing data of WGS and RNA-seq for most of the NextGen models profiled in this study are available in the dbGaP database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/projects/gap/cgi-bin/study.cgi?study_id=phs003444.v4.p1; dbGaP Study accession: phs003444.v4.p1). Raw profiling data (including data for mutation, CN, gene expression and gene dependency) and processed data required for running the custom code used in this study as well as the metadata of the samples are available for download from the DepMap portal (https://depmap.org/portal/data_page/?tab=allData; file set name: ‘NextGen Model Manuscript 2026’). Other analytical results from this study are available in a Figshare collection (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.29472362)75. Some data used in this study were obtained from public repositories. Specifically, in Fig. 1c, tumour mutation data were collected through the cBioPortal (https://www.cbioportal.org/) from the following studies in the TCGA PanCancer Atlas: COAD/READ, PAAD, PRAD and BRCA76; except for the ones labelled with red rectangles, which were acquired from following publications: ref. 60 for the rate of CNS tumour with TERT promoter hotspot mutation; TCGA-COAD/READ58 for the rate of colorectal tumours with chromosome 18q loss; TCGA-PAAD59 or the pancreatic tumour chromosome 9p loss rate; and MSK-MET12 for the rates of colorectal tumours with NRAS hotspot mutation, breast tumours with ESR1 hotspot mutation, and prostate tumours with SPOP damaging mutation. In Fig. 1c,d and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b, GRCh38.p14 human genome assembly (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCF_000001405.40/) was used as the reference sequence in the mutation calls. In Extended Data Fig. 5c, gene expression data for the combined cohort of TCGA, TARGET and GTEx samples (n = 8,167 (normal) and 10,530 (tumour)) were obtained through the UCSC Xena browser (https://xenabrowser.net/; study name: TCGA TARGET GTEx). In Extended Data Fig. 7h, ABSOLUTE tumour purity data of TCGA tumours were compiled from the following publications: ref. 73 and TCGA-PAAD59. Source data are provided with this paper.

Clustering these gene sets by component overlap (>0.3; Extended Data Fig. 8h) merged two sets (adhesion and cytoskeleton (adhesion–cytoskeleton), and cell cycle), whereas five others (lipid metabolism, mTORC1, oxidative phosphorylation, UV response and systemic lupus erythematosus) remained separate.Fig. 5Comparing 2D and 3D dependencies to disentangle the effects of culture conditions.a,b, Gene sets enriched for differential dependencies between 3D and 2D models (n = 94 (3D) and 433 (2D)). Odds ratios for the 9 significant gene sets (q < 0.05) overrepresented in the 200 outlier genes were plotted, clustered and coloured by gene overlap (>0.3; a). Mean dependency differences and their significance for individual genes (two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-test; gene n = 3,521), coloured by the gene set clusters from a were also plotted (b). c–e, Minipool screens were performed to elucidate the differing effects of growth format and culture medium. A minipool screen (250 test genes) was designed (c) to separate the effects of growth format (plastic versus dome) and culture medium (RPMI–FBS versus OPAC) on gene essentiality. The screens identified genes for which dependencies are primarily altered by growth format (d) or culture medium (e), with red dashed lines indicating significance threshold (q = 0.05, two-sided linear regression t-test) and the point colours indicating gene classes in the minipool library (bottom). Screen n = 11 (dome), 7 (plastic), 9 (OPAC), 9 (RPMI–FBS). f,g, Comparisons across growth formats and culture media. f, Different gene classes represented in the minipool library are highlighted. Integrin and actin regulation classes exhibited significant variance across growth formats. g, By contrast, lipid metabolism class were affected by culture medium (q < 0.05, two-tailed F-test; gene n = 200). h, Differential effects on integrin and cholesterol homeostasis dependencies assessed by viability after test gene knockout. Values are the mean ± s.d. (n = 3). P values calculated using two-tailed two-way ANOVA. R–F,

Odds ratios for the 9 significant gene sets (q < 0.05) overrepresented in the 200 outlier genes were plotted, clustered and coloured by gene overlap (>0.3; a). Mean dependency differences and their significance for individual genes (two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-test; gene n = 3,521), coloured by the gene set clusters from a were also plotted (b). c–e, Minipool screens were performed to elucidate the differing effects of growth format and culture medium. The screens identified genes for which dependencies are primarily altered by growth format (d) or culture medium (e), with red dashed lines indicating significance threshold (q = 0.05, two-sided linear regression t-test) and the point colours indicating gene classes in the minipool library (bottom). R–F, RPMI–FBS. i, Colocalization of integrin chains (green) with FAK (red) in KP3 cells under plastic or dome growth conditions (both in RPMI–FBS). Nuclei (blue) and actin (white) are also shown. Representative images from three independent experiments are displayed. Scale bar, 20 μm.

To validate these findings, we knocked out ITB1, ITGAV, MSMO1 or SQLE in KP3 and HS766T pancreas models under 2D plastic (with RPMI–FBS) and 3D dome (with RPMI–FBS or OPAC) cultures. Cholesterol biosynthesis gene dependencies (MSMO1 and SQLE) varied by medium, whereas integrin subunit dependencies (ITGAV and ITGB1) were sensitive to growth format (Fig. 5h and Extended Data Fig. 10a). Immunofluorescence analyses confirmed that integrin β1 (encoded by ITGB1) colocalized with FAK in 3D but not 2D cultures, whereas integrin αV (encoded by ITGAV) showed enhanced FAK colocalization in 2D relative to 3D cultures, which was partially due to reduced cell surface expression in 3D (Fig. 5i and Extended Data Fig. 10b–e). These findings align with their differential roles in cell–ECM interactions across different growth formats55.

For the minipool screens, to evaluate the effects of growth formats and culture media on gene essentiality, we decided to select test genes from nine different functional classes. Most of these gene classes are related to the regulation of adhesion–cytoskeleton, lipid metabolism or other processes highlighted in the systematic comparison of genome-wide CRISPR screen data between 2D models and 3D organoids (Fig. 5a,b). The following gene classes were included: integrin (genes encoding an integrin α or β subunit); ECM adhesion (adhesome, https://adhesome.org/); actin regulation (MSigDB gene set and KEGG regulation of actin cytoskeleton); adherens junction (MSigDB gene set and KEGG adherens junction); tight junction (MSigDB gene set and KEGG tight junction); lipid metabolism (a union of two MSigDB gene sets, Hallmark cholesterol homeostasis and Reactome metabolism of lipids); WNT signalling (MSigDB gene set and GOBP WNT signalling pathway); PI3K–mTOR signalling (MSigDB gene set and Hallmark PI3K–mTOR signalling); cell cycle (MSigDB gene set and GOBP cell cycle); and other genes of particular interest (manual curation). To select 250 test genes from these 9 core functional gene classes, we used the dependency profiles of the gene between 2D models and 3D organoids to prioritize genes that exhibited selective enrichment of dependency in either of these model types. Many of these test genes belong to multiple different classes, and the patterns of membership of individual genes across the nine classes and the number of test genes that exhibit the specific pattern are presented in Extended Data Fig. 9a. We then added 650 non-dependency genes and 100 pan-dependency genes, genes that are universally essential across 2D models and 3D organoids, to compile a list of 1,000 genes (Supplementary Table 3). We subsequently designed 4 enAsCas12a sgRNA sequences for each of these 1,000 genes using the CRISPick web tool (https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gppx/crispick/public), which were assembled into 2 constructs (2 sgRNA sequences for the same gene per construct; 2 constructs per gene) of the pRDA_052 backbone (Addgene, 136474). The resulting library with 2,000 constructs was used for minipool screening.

The viability effect (10 days after sgRNA transduction) of CRISPR-mediated knockout of ITGB1, ITGAV, MSMO1 and SQLE (Fig. 5h and Extended Data Fig. 10a) was assessed using CTG cell viability assays. Specifically, KP3 and HS766T pancreatic cancer cells, both of which were engineered to express enAsCas12a, were infected with several different types of sgRNA-expressing lentivirus on day 0, which included CRISPR cutting controls (sgCh2 and sgAAVS1), sgRNAs targeting common essential genes (sgPOLR2D, sgSF3B1 and sgKIF11) and sgRNAs against the experimental genes (sgITGB1, sgITGAV, sgMSMO1 and sgSQLE). The infected cells were selected with 2 μg ml–1 puromycin between day 1 and day 3. On day 3, cells were trypsinized, counted and reseeded without puromycin. For the 2D monolayer culture on a plastic plate (or plastic culture), cells were seeded at 2,000 cells per well in 100 µl RPMI medium with 10% FBS onto an opaque 96-well plate (Corning, 3903). For the 3D Matrigel dome culture (or dome culture), 10,000 cells were resuspended with 50 μl Matrigel and plated as a dome onto a 12-well plate, which was subsequently incubated (Corning, 356231) at 37 °C for 30 min to allow the Matrigel to solidify. The Matrigel dome was then covered with 1,200 μl per well of either the RPMI medium with 10% FBS or the 1:1 OPAC medium before further incubation. The medium was replaced every 3 days until day 10. Puromycin (2 μg ml–1) was added back to the culture at the first medium replacement.

For Fig. 5g, the variances of dependency between different growth formats and different culture media were scored for all nine of the core functional classes of minipool target genes. The variances were compared between in-class genes and out-of-class genes (that is, rest of the 250 test genes in the minipool library) for each of the 9 core functional classes using one-tailed F-tests. The functional class is considered to be significantly affected by the growth format or culture medium if the corresponding q value was less than 0.05. The numbers of genes in each of the 9 core functional classes are as follows: actin regulation, n = 75; adherens junction, n = 30; cell cycle, n = 53; ECM adhesion, n = 89; integrin, n = 22; lipid metabolism, n = 20; PI3K–mTOR signalling, n = 20; tight junction, n = 34; WNT signalling, n = 29.

For Fig. 5h, the effects of growth formats on the viability of KP3 and HS766T cells following integrin (ITGB1 and ITGAV) knockout, as well as the effects of culture media on the viability of these cells following the knockout of cholesterol synthesis mediators (MSMO1 and SQLE), were analysed by two-tailed two-way ANOVA. The viability of the KP3 and HS766T cells following gene knockout was measured as triplicates.

For Extended Data Fig. 9f,g, effects of growth formats (f) and culture media (g) on gene dependencies (calculated by a linear regression model (see the section ‘Minipool screen analysis’ of the Methods)) were compared between in-class genes and out-of-class genes (that is, the rest of the 250 test genes in the minipool library) for each of the 9 core functional classes of the minipool library. Significance of the difference was assessed by two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-test. The numbers of genes in each of the 9 core functional classes are as follows: actin regulation, n = 75; adherens junction, n = 30; cell cycle, n = 53; ECM adhesion, n = 89; integrin, n = 22; lipid metabolism, n = 20; PI3K–mTOR signalling, n = 20; tight junction, n = 34; and WNT signalling, n = 29.
